mcqs.why: Both the glossary and vocabulary exercise define determination as firmness of purpose and continuing to try despite difficulties, the Quaid's great quality.

lessons.title: Writing
lessons.notes_html:
Writing G — Write an essay on your favourite / ideal personality

  • Q: Q1. Write an essay on your favourite / ideal personality.
    Ans: My favourite and ideal personality is Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah, the founder of Pakistan. In appearance he was tall, dignified and graceful. He always dressed neatly, and when he landed at Mauripur, Karachi, on 7 August 1947, he was wearing a pure white Sherwani. His face was serious and calm, and he rarely showed his feelings in public, yet those who were close to him sometimes saw in his smile the warm-hearted man behind the stern Quaid. His great qualities were honesty, determination, discipline and selflessness. He was a man of very strong feelings and firm principles who never compromised on truth and justice. His attitude towards life was one of hard work, faith and service to the nation; his golden motto was Unity, Faith and Discipline. His achievements are matchless. By the force of his determination and leadership, he turned a defeated people, who had little to hope for under a foreign empire, into a great nation, and won for them an independent homeland, Pakistan, the greatest of the Muslim States and the fifth largest nation in the world. He also taught his people tolerance and equality, declaring that all citizens of Pakistan were free to go to their temples, mosques or any other place of worship. I love and respect the Quaid because he gave us freedom and a country to call our own. He is truly my ideal, and I wish to follow his principles in my own life.

Writing H — Analyse the last paragraph in the text to identify general idea and supporting details

  • Q: Q1. Analyse the last paragraph in the text to identify general idea and supporting details.
    Ans: General idea: In Pakistan all citizens are equal and enjoy complete religious freedom, whatever their religion or caste may be. Supporting details: (1) A few days after he landed in Karachi, Muhammad Ali Jinnah told his people, 'You are free to go to your temples: you are free to go to your mosques or to any other place of worship in this state of Pakistan.' (2) He added, 'You may belong to any religion or caste — we are all citizens of one state.' (3) In saying this, he was reminding them of the Prophet's (peace be upon him) teaching that all men are equal in the eyes of Allah.

Writing I — Write down the summary of the lesson 'Quaid – The Great Leader'

  • Q: Q1. Write down the summary of the lesson 'Quaid – The Great Leader'.
    Ans: On 7 August 1947, Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah landed at Mauripur, Karachi, where a vast, excited crowd welcomed him with slogans of 'Pakistan Zindabad!' He was the founder and first Governor General of Pakistan, the leader who had won a homeland for the Muslims. Through all the cheers and tears of joy, the Quaid remained calm, serious and sober, for he was thinking of the millions who had become homeless and of the thousands who were being attacked and killed while trying to reach Pakistan. In the first year, half a million Muslims were killed or imprisoned and six and a half million took refuge in Pakistan, yet the Quaid still extended the hand of friendship towards India. Though tired and far from well, he had the satisfaction that the greater part of his work was done: by his determination and leadership, seventy million people, who once had no country of their own, had become a great nation. He told his people that all citizens of Pakistan were equal and free to worship in their temples, mosques or any other place of worship, as all men are equal in the eyes of Allah.

Writing J — Translate the following sentences from English to Urdu

  • Q: Translate the following sentences from English to Urdu. 1. There was much in those days of violence to sadden Jinnah who was a man of very strong feelings although he rarely showed it. 2. Seventy million people, who once had no country to call their own, had become a nation — with great ideals and a great faith. 3. Through all the excitement of those first days in the life of the young nation, the man who had made it possible remained calm, serious and sober. 4. As he drove through the great sea of people that stretched from the airport to the city, through all the cheers and tears of joy and the never ending slogans of 'Pakistan Zindabad', the Quaid showed no signs of his feelings. 5. First to step out of the aeroplane was a tall and dignified man wearing a pure white Sherwani.
    Ans: Note: This exercise requires translation into Urdu; translations are not reproduced in these English-only solved notes.

mcqs.q: Who is the favourite and ideal personality in the model essay?
options: Allama Iqbal
Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah, the founder of Pakistan
The writer's teacher
A brave soldier
mcqs.why: The essay begins by naming Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah, the founder of Pakistan, as the writer's favourite and ideal personality.

mcqs.q: According to the essay, what was the Quaid wearing when he landed at Mauripur, Karachi, on 7 August 1947?
options: A dark suit
A uniform
A pure white Sherwani
A white cap and coat
mcqs.why: The essay says he always dressed neatly and, when he landed at Mauripur on 7 August 1947, he was wearing a pure white Sherwani.

mcqs.q: According to the essay, how did the Quaid usually show his feelings in public?
options: He showed them freely to everyone
He rarely showed his feelings in public
He always smiled in public
He never smiled even among friends
mcqs.why: The essay says his face was serious and calm and he rarely showed his feelings in public, though close friends sometimes saw his warm smile.

mcqs.q: Which qualities of the Quaid are listed as his great qualities in the essay?
options: Wealth, fame and power
Honesty, determination, discipline and selflessness
Pride, anger and strictness
Silence, distance and secrecy
mcqs.why: The essay lists honesty, determination, discipline and selflessness as his great qualities, and calls him a man of strong feelings and firm principles.

mcqs.q: What was the Quaid's golden motto, according to the essay?
options: Unity, Faith and Discipline
Faith, Hope and Charity
Work, Worship and Sacrifice
Peace, Progress and Prosperity
mcqs.why: The essay states that his attitude was hard work, faith and service, and his golden motto was Unity, Faith and Discipline.

mcqs.q: According to the essay, what did the Quaid achieve by his determination and leadership?
options: He built the largest empire in the world
He turned a defeated people into a great nation and won Pakistan, the greatest of the Muslim States and the fifth largest nation in the world
He became the richest man in the subcontinent
He ended all violence in the first year
mcqs.why: The essay says he turned a defeated people with little hope under a foreign empire into a great nation and won Pakistan for them.

mcqs.q: What is the general idea of the last paragraph identified in the analysis?
options: That only Muslims are citizens of Pakistan
That Pakistan had become the fifth largest nation
In Pakistan all citizens are equal and enjoy complete religious freedom, whatever their religion or caste
That the Quaid was tired and far from well
mcqs.why: The analysis gives the general idea that in Pakistan all citizens are equal and enjoy complete religious freedom whatever their religion or caste may be.

mcqs.q: Which supporting detail from the Quaid's words is given in the analysis of the last paragraph?
options: 'Pakistan Zindabad! Pakistan Zindabad!'
'You are free to go to your temples: you are free to go to your mosques or to any other place of worship in this state of Pakistan.'
'Unity, Faith and Discipline.'
'The enemy of today may be friend of tomorrow.'
mcqs.why: The analysis supports the general idea with his words that people are free to go to their temples, mosques or any other place of worship in Pakistan.

mcqs.q: According to the summary, how did the Quaid remain through all the cheers and tears of joy?
options: Excited and restless
Calm, serious and sober, thinking of the millions who had become homeless
Happy and carefree about the future
Silent because of his illness alone
mcqs.why: The summary says that through all the cheers and tears of joy the Quaid remained calm, serious and sober, thinking of the millions who had become homeless.

mcqs.q: According to the summary, what did the Quaid do towards India despite the violence and atrocities?
options: He refused all contact with India
He demanded revenge for the killings
He still extended the hand of friendship towards India
He closed the borders permanently
mcqs.why: The summary says that although half a million Muslims were killed or imprisoned, the Quaid still extended the hand of friendship towards India.

lessons.title: Practice Activities
lessons.notes_html:
Listening and Speaking

  • Q: Listening and Speaking — Role play: Make groups and share information and ideas about problems related to the very 1st year of Pakistan.
    Ans: Note: This is an oral classroom activity with no written answer.

lessons.title: Reading and Comprehension
lessons.notes_html:
Pre-Reading

  • Q: Q1. What is nature?
    Ans: Nature is the world around us that is not made by man: the land, hills, valleys, rivers, lakes, trees, flowers, animals, sky and weather. It is the beautiful creation of Allah, which gives us fresh air, food, water and peace of mind.
  • Q: Q2. How do you enjoy the beauty of nature?
    Ans: I enjoy the beauty of nature by going for walks in green fields and gardens, sitting beside a lake or river, and watching flowers, trees and clouds. Beautiful scenes of nature make me feel fresh, calm and happy, and their memory gives me pleasure even afterwards.
  • Q: Q3. Would you like to visit a place of natural beauty?
    Ans: Yes, I would love to visit a place of natural beauty, such as a green valley with a lake and flowers. Such a visit refreshes the mind, removes tiredness and worries, and brings a person closer to nature and to Allah.

Glossary

  • Q: Define 'wandered'.
    Ans: To walk slowly around or to a place, often without any particular sense of purpose or direction.
  • Q: Define 'vales'.
    Ans: Valleys.
  • Q: Define 'host'.
    Ans: A great number or group.
  • Q: Define 'fluttering'.
    Ans: To move lightly and quickly; to make something move in this way.
  • Q: Define 'stretched'.
    Ans: To make something longer, wider or looser, for example by pulling it; to become longer, etc., in this way.
  • Q: Define 'margin'.
    Ans: The edge or border of an area; in the poem, the shore along the edge of the bay where the daffodils grew in a line.
  • Q: Define 'sprightly'.
    Ans: Full of life and energy; lively.
  • Q: Define 'gay'.
    Ans: Light-hearted and carefree; happy and cheerful.
  • Q: Define 'jocund'.
    Ans: Cheerful and light-hearted.
  • Q: Define 'gazed'.
    Ans: To look steadily at somebody or something for a long time, either because you are very interested or surprised, or because you are thinking of something else.
  • Q: Define 'couch'.
    Ans: A long comfortable seat for two or more people to sit on; a sofa or bed.
  • Q: Define 'pensive'.
    Ans: Thinking deeply about something, especially because you are sad or worried.
  • Q: Define 'vacant'.
    Ans: Empty; not being used; (of a mood) with no thoughts, idle.
  • Q: Define 'bay'.
    Ans: A part of the sea, or of a large lake, partly surrounded by a wide curve of the land.
  • Q: Define 'solitude'.
    Ans: The state of being alone, especially when you find this pleasant.
  • Q: Define 'tossing'.
    Ans: To move or make somebody or something move from side to side or up and down.

Comprehension A — Read out the text and answer the following questions

  • Q: Q1. Is there any personification in this poem? If yes, where?
    Ans: Yes, there is personification in the poem, because the daffodils are given human qualities. They are described as a 'crowd' and a 'host', they are 'fluttering and dancing in the breeze', they are 'tossing their heads in sprightly dance', they outdo the waves in glee and are called a 'jocund company'. In the same way, the waves are also shown dancing beside them.
  • Q: Q2. Write at least two lines showing similes.
    Ans: The poem has two clear similes. The first is: 'I wandered lonely as a cloud / That floats on high o'er vales and hills', in which the poet compares himself to a lonely cloud. The second is: 'Continuous as the stars that shine / And twinkle on the Milky Way', in which the daffodils are compared to the endless stars of the Milky Way.
  • Q: Q3. What does the word 'crowd' exactly mean?
    Ans: In the poem, the word 'crowd' does not mean a crowd of people. It means a very large number of daffodils growing closely together in one place, like a crowd of people. The poet uses the word to personify the flowers and to show how many of them there were.
  • Q: Q4. Why does the poet compare himself to a cloud?
    Ans: The poet compares himself to a cloud because, like a cloud floating high over valleys and hills, he was wandering alone and aimlessly, free and detached from the world below. The comparison also shows his loneliness and his closeness to nature at the start of the poem.
  • Q: Q5. Write the main idea of the poem.
    Ans: The main idea of the poem is that the beauty of nature is a lasting source of joy. The poet, wandering alone, suddenly sees a vast host of golden daffodils dancing beside a lake, and the sight fills him with delight. Later, whenever he lies alone in a vacant or pensive mood, the memory of the daffodils flashes upon his inward eye, fills his heart with pleasure, and makes it dance with the daffodils.
  • Q: Q6. Do you like this poem? Why?
    Ans: Yes, I like this poem very much. Its language is simple and musical, and it gives a beautiful picture of golden daffodils dancing beside a lake. It teaches us that the memory of a beautiful scene of nature can give us happiness again and again, even when we are alone or sad.

Comprehension B — Choose the correct option

  • Q: Q1. 'I wandered lonely as a cloud.' Here 'I' refers to ____.
    Options: the reader / the clouds / the poet / the daffodils
    Ans: the poet
  • Q: Q2. 'They stretched in never-ending line / Along the margin of a bay.' Here 'they' refers to ____.
    Options: the clouds / the daffodils / the hills / the stars
    Ans: the daffodils
  • Q: Q3. 'A poet could not but be gay, / In such a jocund company.' Here 'jocund company' refers to the ____.
    Options: friends of the poet / daffodils / clouds / stars
    Ans: daffodils
  • Q: Q4. In the first stanza what was the poet doing?
    Options: walking aimlessly / writing a poem / looking at the clouds / looking at the stars
    Ans: walking aimlessly
  • Q: Q5. 'What wealth the show to me had brought.' By 'wealth' the poet means ____.
    Options: company / gold / pleasure / money
    Ans: pleasure

mcqs.q: 'I wandered lonely as a cloud.' Here 'I' refers to ____.
options: the reader
the poet
the clouds
the daffodils
mcqs.why: The word 'I' is the speaker of the poem, William Wordsworth himself, who describes wandering alone like a cloud over vales and hills.

mcqs.q: 'They stretched in never-ending line / Along the margin of a bay.' Here 'they' refers to ____.
options: the clouds
the hills
the stars
the daffodils
mcqs.why: The lines describe the daffodils stretching in a never-ending line along the margin of the bay, so 'they' clearly refers to the daffodils.

mcqs.q: 'A poet could not but be gay, / In such a jocund company.' Here 'jocund company' refers to the ____.
options: daffodils
friends of the poet
clouds
stars
mcqs.why: The cheerful, light-hearted company that makes the poet gay is the host of dancing daffodils beside the lake, not his human friends.

mcqs.q: In the first stanza what was the poet doing?
options: writing a poem
looking at the clouds
walking aimlessly
looking at the stars
mcqs.why: In the first stanza the poet was wandering lonely as a cloud, that is, walking aimlessly without a fixed purpose or direction.

mcqs.q: 'What wealth the show to me had brought.' By 'wealth' the poet means ____.
options: company
gold
money
pleasure
mcqs.why: By 'wealth' the poet does not mean money or gold; he means the lasting pleasure and happiness the sight of the daffodils brought him.

mcqs.q: What does the word 'wandered' mean in the poem?
options: To look steadily at something for a long time
To walk slowly around, often without any particular purpose or direction
To move lightly and quickly in the breeze
To pull something to make it longer or wider
mcqs.why: The glossary defines 'wandered' as walking slowly around or to a place, often without any particular sense of purpose or direction.

mcqs.q: Where is personification found in the poem?
options: The poet compares himself to a lonely cloud
The daffodils are called a crowd and a host and are shown fluttering, dancing and tossing their heads
The daffodils are compared to the stars of the Milky Way
The poet lies on his couch in a pensive mood
mcqs.why: Personification gives the daffodils human qualities: they form a crowd and a host, flutter and dance, toss their heads and outdo the waves in glee.

mcqs.q: Which lines contain a simile comparing the poet himself?
options: Continuous as the stars that shine and twinkle on the Milky Way
Ten thousand saw I at a glance, tossing their heads in sprightly dance
I wandered lonely as a cloud that floats on high o'er vales and hills
Fluttering and dancing in the breeze beside the lake
mcqs.why: The poet compares himself to a lonely cloud floating high over vales and hills, using 'as' to show his loneliness and aimless wandering.

mcqs.q: What does the word 'host' mean in the poem?
options: A long comfortable seat for two or more people
The edge or border of an area
A great number or group
The state of being alone and finding it pleasant
mcqs.why: In the glossary 'host' means a great number or group, which is how the poet describes the vast crowd of golden daffodils he suddenly saw.

mcqs.q: What is the main idea of the poem 'The Daffodils'?
options: Nature's beauty is a lasting source of joy whose memory gives pleasure again in solitude
A poet should always walk beside lakes in spring
Clouds are lonelier than human beings
Daffodils are more valuable than gold and money
mcqs.why: The main idea is that the beauty of nature gives lasting joy: the memory of the daffodils flashes on the inward eye and fills the heart with pleasure.

lessons.title: Language Focus
lessons.notes_html:
Vocabulary A — Deduce the meaning of the following words. Confirm your meaning from the dictionary

  • Q: Define 'oft'.
    Ans: Often. 'For oft, when on my couch I lie' means 'for often, when I lie on my couch'.
  • Q: Define 'never-ending'.
    Ans: Without an end; going on for ever. The daffodils 'stretched in never-ending line' along the bay.
  • Q: Define 'glee'.
    Ans: Great delight, joy and merriment. The daffodils outdid the sparkling waves 'in glee'.
  • Q: Define 'bliss'.
    Ans: Perfect happiness and pleasure. The memory of the daffodils is called 'the bliss of solitude'.
  • Q: Define 'twinkle'.
    Ans: To shine with a light that keeps changing between bright and faint, like stars. The stars 'twinkle on the Milky Way'.
  • Q: Define 'sparkling'.
    Ans: Shining brightly with flashes of light. The waves beside the daffodils are 'sparkling waves'.
  • Q: Define 'stretch'.
    Ans: To spread out or extend over a long distance. The daffodils 'stretched in never-ending line along the margin of a bay'.

Vocabulary B — Can you tell which lines of the poem indicate

  • Q: Q1. Which lines of the poem indicate the comparison of daffodils with stars?
    Ans: 'Continuous as the stars that shine / And twinkle on the Milky Way, / They stretched in never-ending line / Along the margin of a bay.'
  • Q: Q2. Which lines of the poem indicate the speaker's solitariness to that of a cloud?
    Ans: 'I wandered lonely as a cloud / That floats on high o'er vales and hills.'
  • Q: Q3. Which lines of the poem indicate the comparison of daffodils to a crowd of people?
    Ans: 'When all at once I saw a crowd, / A host, of golden daffodils.'
  • Q: Q4. Which lines of the poem indicate the comparison of daffodils to dancing humans?
    Ans: 'Beside the lake, beneath the trees, / Fluttering and dancing in the breeze' and 'Tossing their heads in sprightly dance.'

Vocabulary C — Which word of the poem means the same as

  • Q: Q1. Which word of the poem means the same as 'number of daffodils'?
    Ans: host (the poet also gives the number as 'Ten thousand saw I at a glance').
  • Q: Q2. Which word of the poem means the same as 'glance'?
    Ans: glance ('Ten thousand saw I at a glance' — a quick look).
  • Q: Q3. Which word of the poem means the same as 'happy feeling'?
    Ans: glee (also 'gay' and 'jocund' express the same happy feeling).
  • Q: Q4. Which word of the poem means the same as 'deep thought'?
    Ans: pensive ('In vacant or in pensive mood' — deep in thought).
  • Q: Q5. Which word of the poem means the same as 'blessing'?
    Ans: bliss ('Which is the bliss of solitude' — a blessing and perfect happiness).

Grammar A — Use the correct form of the (present / past) participle to fill in the blanks

  • Q: Q1. His ____ coat needs mending.
    Options: tattered / tattering / tatter / tatters
    Ans: tattered
  • Q: Q2. A ____ stone gathers no moss.
    Options: rolling / rolled / roll / rolls
    Ans: rolling
  • Q: Q3. A ____ opportunity never returns.
    Options: losing / lost / loss / lose
    Ans: lost
  • Q: Q4. He kept me ____.
    Options: waiting / waited / wait / waits
    Ans: waiting
  • Q: Q5. She looked ____.
    Options: worried / worrying / worry / worries
    Ans: worried

Grammar B — Fill in the correct participle form (Present Participle, Past Participle)

  • Q: He was sitting in an armchair ____ a magazine.
    Ans: reading
  • Q: ____ in the company for many years, he knew everyone and everything.
    Ans: Having worked
  • Q: The cup with milk ____ on the table.
    Ans: placed
  • Q: ____ each other for ages, they had a lot to talk about.
    Ans: Not having seen
  • Q: ____ into a rich family, she got everything she wished for.
    Ans: Born

Grammar C — Underline the infinitive in each sentence

  • Q: Q1. Underline the infinitive in the sentence: 'The best plumber to call is Mr. Amir.'
    Ans: The infinitive is 'to call'. The complete sentence is: The best plumber to call is Mr. Amir.
  • Q: Q2. Underline the infinitive in the sentence: 'His only ambition was to succeed at his job.'
    Ans: The infinitive is 'to succeed'. The complete sentence is: His only ambition was to succeed at his job.
  • Q: Q3. Underline the infinitive in the sentence: 'Each year Mansoor tried to find more deductions for his tax return.'
    Ans: The infinitive is 'to find'. The complete sentence is: Each year Mansoor tried to find more deductions for his tax return.
  • Q: Q4. Underline the infinitive in the sentence: 'To patch the hole in the tyre, the mechanic inserted a plug.'
    Ans: The infinitive is 'To patch'. The complete sentence is: To patch the hole in the tyre, the mechanic inserted a plug.
  • Q: Q5. Underline the infinitive in the sentence: 'She learnt to read and write English in coaching academy.'
    Ans: The infinitives are 'to read' and '(to) write'. The complete sentence is: She learnt to read and write English in coaching academy.

Grammar D — Combine the following simple sentences into a single simple sentence by using an infinitive

  • Q: Q1. Combine into a single simple sentence by using an infinitive: 'I have engaged a private tutor. He will teach me English.'
    Ans: I have engaged a private tutor to teach me English.
  • Q: Q2. Combine into a single simple sentence by using an infinitive: 'He is very weak. He cannot walk.'
    Ans: He is too weak to walk.
  • Q: Q3. Combine into a single simple sentence by using an infinitive: 'I looked out of the window of my carriage. I wanted to see the green pastures.'
    Ans: I looked out of the window of my carriage to see the green pastures.
  • Q: Q4. Combine into a single simple sentence by using an infinitive: 'The proposal is quite unreasonable. It cannot be accepted.'
    Ans: The proposal is too unreasonable to be accepted.
  • Q: Q5. Combine into a single simple sentence by using an infinitive: 'He wants to gain the first position. He works hard for it.'
    Ans: He works hard to gain the first position.

Grammar E — Underline the gerund or gerund phrase in the following sentences

  • Q: Q1. Underline the gerund or gerund phrase in the sentence: 'Swimming at beach is safer than swimming in open sea.'
    Ans: The gerund phrases are 'Swimming at beach' and 'swimming in open sea'. Both are used as nouns: the first as subject and the second as object of the preposition 'than'.
  • Q: Q2. Underline the gerund or gerund phrase in the sentence: 'Kareem doesn't like getting up early on Sunday.'
    Ans: The gerund phrase is 'getting up early on Sunday'. It is used as a noun, the object of the verb 'like'.
  • Q: Q3. Underline the gerund or gerund phrase in the sentence: 'Maria enjoys reading stories at night.'
    Ans: The gerund phrase is 'reading stories at night'. It is used as a noun, the object of the verb 'enjoys'.
  • Q: Q4. Underline the gerund or gerund phrase in the sentence: 'Leaving Swat changed Nazeer's career forever.'
    Ans: The gerund phrase is 'Leaving Swat'. It is used as a noun, the subject of the verb 'changed'.
  • Q: Q5. Underline the gerund or gerund phrase in the sentence: 'The darkness of the night prevented us from finishing the job.'
    Ans: The gerund is 'finishing' (in the gerund phrase 'finishing the job'). It is used as a noun, the object of the preposition 'from'.

mcqs.q: His ____ coat needs mending.
options: tattering
tattered
tatter
tatters
mcqs.why: A coat that has been damaged needs the past participle 'tattered' as an adjective; 'tattering' would mean it is actively tearing something else.

mcqs.q: A ____ stone gathers no moss.
options: rolled
roll
rolling
rolls
mcqs.why: The proverb needs the present participle 'rolling' because the stone is actively rolling and therefore gathers no moss on its surface.

mcqs.q: A ____ opportunity never returns.
options: losing
loss
lose
lost
mcqs.why: An opportunity that is gone needs the past participle 'lost'; once it has been lost, such an opportunity never returns to us.

mcqs.q: He kept me ____.
options: waiting
waited
wait
waits
mcqs.why: After 'kept me' the present participle 'waiting' is correct because the person was kept in the continuing state of waiting for someone.

mcqs.q: She looked ____.
options: worrying
worry
worried
worries
mcqs.why: She herself felt the emotion, so the past participle 'worried' is correct; 'worrying' would describe something that causes worry to others.

mcqs.q: What does the word 'oft' mean in 'For oft, when on my couch I lie'?
options: Seldom
Never
Often
Always at night
mcqs.why: The vocabulary note explains that 'oft' is the older poetic form of 'often', so the line means 'for often, when I lie on my couch'.

mcqs.q: What does the word 'glee' mean in the poem?
options: Perfect happiness felt only in solitude
Great delight, joy and merriment
A light that keeps changing between bright and faint
A deep and thoughtful mood
mcqs.why: The vocabulary section defines 'glee' as great delight, joy and merriment, which is why the daffodils outdid the sparkling waves in glee.

mcqs.q: Which word of the poem means the same as 'deep thought'?
options: glee
bliss
vacant
pensive
mcqs.why: The poem uses 'pensive' for deep thought, as in 'in vacant or in pensive mood', where the poet lies thinking deeply about something.

mcqs.q: Which word of the poem means the same as 'number of daffodils'?
options: host
glance
margin
couch
mcqs.why: The word 'host' means a great number, and the poet also gives the number directly when he says 'Ten thousand saw I at a glance'.

mcqs.q: Complete the sentence with the correct participle: 'He was sitting in an armchair ____ a magazine.'
options: placed
reading
Having worked
Born
mcqs.why: The solved exercise uses the present participle 'reading' because he was actively reading the magazine while sitting in the armchair.

mcqs.q: Complete the sentence with the correct participle: '____ in the company for many years, he knew everyone and everything.'
options: Reading
Placed
Having worked
Not having seen
mcqs.why: The perfect participle 'Having worked' is correct because the long period of work in the company was completed before he knew everyone.

mcqs.q: What is the infinitive in 'His only ambition was to succeed at his job'?
options: His only ambition
was
at his job
to succeed
mcqs.why: The infinitive is 'to succeed', formed with 'to' plus the base verb, and it completes the meaning of his only ambition in the sentence.

mcqs.q: Combine into one simple sentence using an infinitive: 'He is very weak. He cannot walk.'
options: He is very weak and he cannot walk.
He is too weak to walk.
He is weak because he cannot walk.
He cannot walk so he is very weak.
mcqs.why: The solved combination uses 'too ... to' with the infinitive: 'He is too weak to walk', joining both ideas into a single simple sentence.

mcqs.q: What is the gerund phrase in 'Maria enjoys reading stories at night'?
options: Maria enjoys
reading stories at night
at night
enjoys reading
mcqs.why: The gerund phrase 'reading stories at night' works as a noun and is the object of the verb 'enjoys' in this solved grammar exercise.

mcqs.q: What does the word 'bliss' mean in 'the bliss of solitude'?
options: Great delight shown in dancing
A quick look at something
Perfect happiness and pleasure
A state of deep worried thought
mcqs.why: The vocabulary section defines 'bliss' as perfect happiness and pleasure, and the memory of the daffodils is called the bliss of solitude.

lessons.title: Writing
lessons.notes_html:
Writing A — Paraphrase the second stanza of the poem 'The Daffodils'

  • Q: Q1. Paraphrase the second stanza of the poem 'The Daffodils'.
    Ans: The poet says that the daffodils were as countless and continuous as the stars that shine and twinkle in the Milky Way. They spread out in a line that seemed to have no end, along the shore of the bay. At a single glance he saw about ten thousand of them, tossing their heads and dancing in a lively manner.
  • Q: Q2. Paraphrase the whole poem 'The Daffodils' in your own words.
    Ans: Stanza 1: I was wandering alone, like a lonely cloud floating high over valleys and hills, when suddenly I saw a large crowd, a great host, of golden daffodils growing beside the lake and under the trees, moving lightly and dancing in the breeze. Stanza 2: The daffodils were as continuous as the stars that shine and twinkle in the Milky Way, and they stretched in a never-ending line along the edge of the bay; at one glance I saw ten thousand of them, tossing their heads in a lively dance. Stanza 3: The waves beside them also danced, but the daffodils surpassed the sparkling waves in joy and delight; a poet could not help being happy in such cheerful company, and I kept looking at them, little knowing at that time what great wealth (pleasure) this sight had brought me. Stanza 4: For often, when I lie on my couch in an idle or thoughtful mood, the daffodils appear before my mind's eye, which is the true blessing of being alone, and then my heart fills with pleasure and dances with the daffodils.

Writing B — Now write the summary of the poem, The Daffodils

  • Q: Q1. Write the summary of the poem, The Daffodils.
    Ans: William Wordsworth, wandering alone like a cloud over valleys and hills, suddenly sees a vast host of golden daffodils beside a lake, fluttering and dancing in the breeze. They stretch in a never-ending line along the bay like the stars of the Milky Way, about ten thousand at a glance, tossing their heads in a lively dance and outdoing even the sparkling waves in glee. The poet gazes at them in delight, little knowing their worth. Afterwards, whenever he lies alone in a vacant or pensive mood, the scene flashes upon his inward eye, fills his heart with pleasure, and makes it dance with the daffodils. Thus the memory of nature's beauty becomes a lasting treasure of happiness.

mcqs.q: According to the paraphrase of the second stanza, the daffodils were as continuous as what?
options: The waves dancing beside the lake
The stars that shine and twinkle in the Milky Way
A crowd of people in a city street
The clouds floating over the hills
mcqs.why: The paraphrase says the daffodils were as countless and continuous as the stars that shine and twinkle in the Milky Way above.

mcqs.q: How many daffodils did the poet see at a single glance, according to the paraphrase?
options: About one thousand
About ten thousand
About one hundred
About ten
mcqs.why: Both the paraphrase and the summary state that at a single glance the poet saw about ten thousand daffodils tossing their heads.

mcqs.q: In the paraphrase of the second stanza, where did the daffodils spread out?
options: Across the tops of the hills
Under the trees only
In a never-ending line along the shore of the bay
Around the poet's couch at home
mcqs.why: The paraphrase explains that they spread out in a line that seemed to have no end, along the shore or margin of the bay.

mcqs.q: In the summary, who is the poet wandering like a cloud over valleys and hills?
options: The reader of the poem
William Wordsworth
A lonely traveller
The gardener beside the lake
mcqs.why: The summary begins by naming William Wordsworth, wandering alone like a cloud, as the poet who suddenly sees the host of daffodils.

mcqs.q: According to the summary, what did the daffodils outdo in glee?
options: The stars of the Milky Way
The clouds in the sky
The sparkling waves
The trees beside the lake
mcqs.why: The summary states that the daffodils were tossing their heads in a lively dance and outdoing even the sparkling waves in glee.

mcqs.q: According to the summary, what happens when the poet lies in a vacant or pensive mood?
options: He forgets the daffodils completely
He writes a new poem at once
He goes back to the lake immediately
The scene flashes upon his inward eye and fills his heart with pleasure
mcqs.why: The summary says the scene flashes upon his inward eye, fills his heart with pleasure and makes it dance with the daffodils.

mcqs.q: According to the paraphrase of the third stanza, what did the poet little know at the time?
options: What great wealth, or pleasure, the sight had brought him
How many stars are in the Milky Way
Why the waves were sparkling
Where the bay ended
mcqs.why: The paraphrase explains that he kept looking in delight, little knowing at that time what great wealth, meaning pleasure, the sight had brought.

mcqs.q: How does the summary describe the line of daffodils along the bay?
options: As a short row beside the trees
As a never-ending line like the stars of the Milky Way
As a circle around the lake
As a single row behind the hills
mcqs.why: The summary describes them stretching in a never-ending line along the bay, just like the continuous stars of the Milky Way.

mcqs.q: What were the daffodils doing in the paraphrase of the first stanza?
options: Sleeping beneath the trees
Falling into the lake
Moving lightly and dancing in the breeze
Hiding behind the clouds
mcqs.why: The paraphrase of the first stanza says the golden daffodils beside the lake and under the trees were moving lightly and dancing in the breeze.

mcqs.q: What conclusion does the summary reach at the end?
options: Daffodils should be picked and kept at home
Solitude is always sad and empty
Walking alone is a waste of time
The memory of nature's beauty becomes a lasting treasure of happiness
mcqs.why: The summary ends by concluding that the memory of nature's beauty becomes a lasting treasure of happiness for the poet.

lessons.title: Practice Activities
lessons.notes_html:
Listening and Speaking

  • Q: Listening and Speaking — Develop and practice a dialogue in group to exhibit appropriate convention of interruption.
    Ans: Note: This is an oral classroom activity with no written answer.

lessons.title: Reading and Comprehension
lessons.notes_html:
Pre-Reading

  • Q: Look at the mind map below to predict the content of the lesson. (Mind map centre: Peaceful Co-existence, linked to: Freedom and safety, Religious harmony, Humanity and justice, Patience and tolerance, Love and peace)
    Ans: The mind map suggests that the lesson is about how different communities can live together in peace. It will probably explain how Hazrat Muhammad (peace be upon him) established peaceful co-existence in Madina through religious harmony, humanity and justice, patience and tolerance, and love and peace, so that every community enjoyed freedom and safety.

Glossary

  • Q: Define 'abolish'.
    Ans: To officially end a law, a system or an institution.
  • Q: Define 'abandon'.
    Ans: To leave somebody, especially somebody you are responsible for, with no intention of returning.
  • Q: Define 'charter'.
    Ans: A written statement describing the rights that a particular group of people should have.
  • Q: Define 'community'.
    Ans: All the people who live in a particular area, country, etc. when talked about as a group.
  • Q: Define 'converts'.
    Ans: To change or make somebody change their religion or beliefs.
  • Q: Define 'harmony'.
    Ans: A state of peaceful existence and agreement.
  • Q: Define 'inhabited'.
    Ans: With people or animals living there.
  • Q: Define 'kith and kin'.
    Ans: Friends and relatives.
  • Q: Define 'liability'.
    Ans: The state of being legally responsible for something.
  • Q: Define 'migrated'.
    Ans: To move from one part of the world to another.
  • Q: Define 'thick and thin'.
    Ans: Even when there are problems or difficulties.
  • Q: Define 'signatory'.
    Ans: A person, a country or an organization that has signed an official agreement.

Comprehension A — Answer the following questions

  • Q: Q1. Why did the Holy Prophet Hazrat Muhammad (peace be upon him) abolish the tribal distinction in Medina?
    Ans: Hazrat Muhammad (peace be upon him) abolished the tribal distinction in order to create harmony and co-operation among the people of Madina. He grouped all the inhabitants under one general name so that they could live as one community. He knew that the goodwill and support of all sections of the people were necessary for the creation of an Islamic state.
  • Q: Q2. What did UN adopt unanimously?
    Ans: In 1948, the General Assembly of the United Nations unanimously adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. The declaration proclaims the religious, personal, civic, political, economic, social and cultural rights of human beings. This charter was approved on 10th December, 1948 and contains thirty points in all.
  • Q: Q3. How do we know that Islam is the protector of Human Rights?
    Ans: We know this because the clauses of the Madina Charter were later incorporated in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights by the UN. Long before the UN declaration, the Madina Charter had already announced civic equality, freedom of worship and religious and racial tolerance. This shows that Islam protected human rights many centuries before the modern world recognized them.
  • Q: Q4. Define tolerance and give examples from the text.
    Ans: Tolerance means allowing other people to follow their own religion, beliefs and way of life without interference, and living with them patiently and peacefully. The text gives clear examples: the Muslims, the Jews and other communities of Madina were free to profess their own respective religion and perform their religious ceremonies. It also states that the individual offence of a non-Muslim would not bring liability on his whole community, and that the oppressed should be protected.
  • Q: Q5. We must always honour our words. Why?
    Ans: We must always honour our words because agreements and promises create trust among people and communities. The Madina Charter worked because all the signatory communities accepted its clauses and stood by them, even defending one another collectively when attacked. If people break their word, trust is destroyed, disputes increase and peace cannot survive.
  • Q: Q6. Write an account of an act of tolerance you have shown / seen.
    Ans: Last year a new student joined our class who belonged to a different area and spoke a different dialect, and some boys made fun of his accent. I did not join them; instead I sat with him, helped him with the class work and asked the others to imagine how they would feel in a strange place. Within a few weeks he had become a good friend of the whole class. This small act of patience and acceptance taught me that tolerance turns strangers into friends.

Comprehension B — Choose the correct answer

  • Q: Q1. The faithful followers of Muhammad (peace be upon him) who had abandoned the ties of kith and kin and followed him (peace be upon him). In the sentence above, the phrase 'abandoned the ties' means ________.
    Options: held onto relationships / kept relationships / gave up relationships / maintained relationships
    Ans: gave up relationships
  • Q: Q2. The new converts of Medina who had helped the Prophet (peace be upon him) through thick and thin were known as Ansar. In the sentence above, 'new converts of Medina' refers to ________.
    Options: the people of Medina, who newly accepted Islam / the people who newly migrated to Medina / the people of Medina, who newly refused to accept Islam / the people who left Medina to accept Islam
    Ans: the people of Medina, who newly accepted Islam
  • Q: Q3. The Muslims, the Jews and other communities of this republic should be free to profess their own respective religion. The opposite word of the word 'profess' in this sentence is ________.
    Options: own up / give up / put up / take up
    Ans: give up
  • Q: Q4. Which of the following is not a clause of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights by the UN?
    Options: We are all free and equal, we are all born free. / We all have the right to live, and to live in freedom and safety. / Everybody has the right to hurt or to torture each other. / Education is a right, primary education should be free.
    Ans: Everybody has the right to hurt or to torture each other.
  • Q: Q5. The oppressed should be protected. The word 'oppressed' in this sentence means ________.
    Options: free / ill-treated / untroubled / exempted
    Ans: ill-treated

Comprehension C — Use the following words in sentences of your own

  • Q: Use 'harmony' in a sentence of your own.
    Ans: People of different faiths live in complete harmony in our town.
  • Q: Use 'abolish' in a sentence of your own.
    Ans: The government has decided to abolish the old tax on textbooks.
  • Q: Use 'tyrannized' in a sentence of your own.
    Ans: The cruel ruler tyrannized his people for many years until they rose against him.
  • Q: Use 'trivial' in a sentence of your own.
    Ans: We should not waste our time quarrelling over trivial matters.
  • Q: Use 'tolerance' in a sentence of your own.
    Ans: Tolerance towards other religions is a basic teaching of the Madina Charter.

mcqs.q: The faithful followers of Muhammad (peace be upon him) who had abandoned the ties of kith and kin and followed him (peace be upon him). In the sentence above, the phrase 'abandoned the ties' means ________.
options: held onto relationships
gave up relationships
kept relationships
maintained relationships
mcqs.why: To abandon ties of kith and kin means to give up those relationships, as the Muhajireen left their friends and relatives in Makkah.

mcqs.q: The new converts of Medina who had helped the Prophet (peace be upon him) through thick and thin were known as Ansar. In the sentence above, 'new converts of Medina' refers to ________.
options: the people who newly migrated to Medina
the people of Medina, who newly refused to accept Islam
the people of Medina, who newly accepted Islam
the people who left Medina to accept Islam
mcqs.why: The Ansar were the people of Medina itself who newly accepted Islam and then helped the Prophet through good and bad times.

mcqs.q: The Muslims, the Jews and other communities of this republic should be free to profess their own respective religion. The opposite word of the word 'profess' in this sentence is ________.
options: own up
put up
take up
give up
mcqs.why: To profess a religion means to declare and follow it openly, so its opposite here is 'give up', meaning to stop following it.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is not a clause of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights by the UN?
options: Everybody has the right to hurt or to torture each other.
We are all free and equal, we are all born free.
We all have the right to live, and to live in freedom and safety.
Education is a right, primary education should be free.
mcqs.why: The UN declaration protects people from hurt and torture; it never gives anybody a right to hurt or torture others, unlike the other clauses.

mcqs.q: The oppressed should be protected. The word 'oppressed' in this sentence means ________.
options: free
untroubled
ill-treated
exempted
mcqs.why: The oppressed are people who are ill-treated and crushed by others, which is exactly why the Charter says they should be protected.

mcqs.q: Why did Hazrat Muhammad (peace be upon him) abolish the tribal distinction in Madina?
options: To punish the tribes of Madina
To create harmony and co-operation and group the inhabitants as one community
To make one tribe rule over all the others
To separate the Muslims from the Jews
mcqs.why: He abolished tribal distinction to create harmony and co-operation, grouping all inhabitants under one general name as a single community.

mcqs.q: What did the United Nations adopt in 1948, and how many points does it contain?
options: The Madina Charter, with ten points
A trade agreement, with twenty points
The Universal Declaration of Human Rights, with thirty points
A peace treaty, with forty points
mcqs.why: In 1948 the UN General Assembly unanimously adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, approved on 10 December 1948 with thirty points.

mcqs.q: What is a 'charter', according to the glossary?
options: A person who has signed an official agreement
A written statement describing the rights that a particular group of people should have
A state of peaceful existence and agreement
The state of being legally responsible for something
mcqs.why: The glossary defines a charter as a written statement describing the rights that a particular group of people should have.

mcqs.q: What does 'signatory' mean in the lesson?
options: A person, country or organization that has signed an official agreement
A person who has changed his religion or beliefs
A person who has moved to another part of the world
A friend or relative of the Prophet (peace be upon him)
mcqs.why: A signatory is a person, country or organization that has signed an official agreement, as the communities signed the Madina Charter.

mcqs.q: Which example of tolerance is given in the lesson?
options: Every offence was punished by the whole community
Only one religion could be practised in Madina
Disputes were settled by fighting
Muslims, Jews and other communities were free to profess their own religion and perform their ceremonies
mcqs.why: Tolerance is shown by the Charter allowing Muslims, Jews and other communities to profess their own religion and perform their ceremonies freely.

lessons.title: Language Focus
lessons.notes_html:
Vocabulary A — Search the text for the phrases meaning the same as

  • Q: Find in the text a phrase meaning 'relatives'.
    Ans: kith and kin
  • Q: Find in the text a word meaning 'peaceful co-existence'.
    Ans: harmony
  • Q: Find in the text a phrase meaning 'good and bad times'.
    Ans: through thick and thin
  • Q: Find in the text the expression for 'freedom' (of worship).
    Ans: The text expresses it as being 'free' — all communities 'should be free to profess their own respective religion', that is, they had freedom of worship.

Grammar A — Use the words in brackets to write a possible answer to each question in the present perfect continuous tense

  • Q: Q1. Why is Ali at night school? (learn, french)
    Ans: He has been learning how to speak French. (Given in the book as the example.)
  • Q: Q2. Why hasn't Abrar done his homework? (take, dogs, walk)
    Ans: He has been taking the dogs for a walk.
  • Q: Q3. Why did Nawab buy you a present? (help, project)
    Ans: I have been helping him with his project.
  • Q: Q4. Why is Shehla busy on Saturday? (go, cooking lesson)
    Ans: She has been going to cooking lessons.
  • Q: Q5. Why are you so angry? (wait, four hours)
    Ans: I have been waiting for four hours.
  • Q: Q6. How long has Gul Khan been an artist? (paint, since high school) [Printed as '5.' again in the book.]
    Ans: He has been painting since high school.

Grammar B — Make past perfect continuous tense by using correct form of verb

  • Q: She ____ (sleep) for ten hours when I awoke her.
    Ans: had been sleeping
  • Q: They ____ (live) in Bannu for three years when he lost his job.
    Ans: had been living
  • Q: They ____ (wait) at the station for 90 minutes when the train finally arrived.
    Ans: had been waiting
  • Q: They were very tired in the evening because they ____ (help) on the farm all day.
    Ans: had been helping
  • Q: Tahir ____ (cycle) so his legs were sore in the evening.
    Ans: had been cycling

Revision — Exercise 1: Common noun or proper noun

  • Q: Classify 'author' and give a related noun.
    Ans: Common noun — related proper noun: William Shakespeare.
  • Q: Classify 'mountain' and give a related noun.
    Ans: Common noun — related proper noun: K2.
  • Q: Classify 'teacher' and give a related noun.
    Ans: Common noun — related proper noun: Prof. Kamal.
  • Q: Classify 'Prof. Kamal' and give a related noun.
    Ans: Proper noun — related common noun: teacher.
  • Q: Classify 'building' and give a related noun.
    Ans: Common noun — related proper noun: Islamia College (the building).
  • Q: Classify 'eid' (Eid) and give a related noun.
    Ans: Proper noun — related common noun: festival.
  • Q: Classify 'park' and give a related noun.
    Ans: Common noun — related proper noun: Jinnah Park.
  • Q: Classify 'friend' and give a related noun.
    Ans: Common noun — related proper noun: Ali.
  • Q: Classify 'city' and give a related noun.
    Ans: Common noun — related proper noun: Karachi.
  • Q: Classify 'river' and give a related noun.
    Ans: Common noun — related proper noun: the Indus River.
  • Q: Classify 'Islamia college' (Islamia College) and give a related noun.
    Ans: Proper noun — related common noun: college.
  • Q: Classify 'France' and give a related noun.
    Ans: Proper noun — related common noun: country.
  • Q: Classify 'Karachi' and give a related noun.
    Ans: Proper noun — related common noun: city.
  • Q: Classify 'hero' and give a related noun.
    Ans: Common noun — related proper noun: Quaid-e-Azam.
  • Q: Classify 'boy' and give a related noun.
    Ans: Common noun — related proper noun: Ahmed.

Revision — Exercise 2: Identify the collective nouns and use them in new sentences

  • Q: i. The staff quickly responded to the alarm. Identify the collective noun and use it in a new sentence.
    Ans: Collective noun: staff. New sentence: The staff of our school works very hard for the students.
  • Q: ii. The audience stood up and chaired the speaker. Identify the collective noun and use it in a new sentence.
    Ans: Collective noun: audience. New sentence: The audience listened to the speech in complete silence.
  • Q: iii. Suddenly the class became very quiet. Identify the collective noun and use it in a new sentence.
    Ans: Collective noun: class. New sentence: Our class is going on a study tour next week.
  • Q: iv. The board met last night to vote on the budget. Identify the collective noun and use it in a new sentence.
    Ans: Collective noun: board. New sentence: The board of directors approved the new plan.
  • Q: v. Her family is going to Nathiagali this weekend. Identify the collective noun and use it in a new sentence.
    Ans: Collective noun: family. New sentence: My family lives in a small village near Peshawar.

Revision — Exercise 3: Make plural of the following nouns

  • Q: Give the plural of 'arm'.
    Ans: arms
  • Q: Give the plural of 'brother-in-law'.
    Ans: brothers-in-law
  • Q: Give the plural of 'court room'.
    Ans: court rooms
  • Q: Give the plural of 'shoe lace'.
    Ans: shoe laces
  • Q: Give the plural of 'Commander-in-chief'.
    Ans: Commanders-in-chief
  • Q: Which of these nouns also changes meaning in the plural?
    Ans: 'Arm' changes meaning in the plural: 'arm' is a part of the body, but 'arms' can also mean weapons. The other nouns keep the same meaning in the plural and only show more than one in number.

Revision — Exercise 4: Sort out uncountable nouns and use them in sentences

  • Q: Sort out the uncountable nouns from: sugar, mango, start, flour, bread, orange, milk, tea, chocolate, candy.
    Ans: The uncountable nouns are: sugar, flour, bread, milk, tea and chocolate. The countable nouns are: mango, start, orange and candy.
  • Q: Use 'sugar' in a sentence.
    Ans: Please put two spoons of sugar in my tea.
  • Q: Use 'flour' in a sentence.
    Ans: Mother kneaded the flour to make bread.
  • Q: Use 'bread' in a sentence.
    Ans: We eat fresh bread for breakfast every morning.
  • Q: Use 'milk' in a sentence.
    Ans: Milk is very good for the health of children.
  • Q: Use 'tea' in a sentence.
    Ans: A hot cup of tea refreshes us in cold weather.
  • Q: Use 'chocolate' in a sentence.
    Ans: She melted some chocolate to decorate the cake.

Revision — Exercise 5: Write three sentences having noun phrases

  • Q: Write three sentences having noun phrases and underline (identify) the noun phrase in each.
    Ans: (1) 'The brave soldiers of our army' guard our borders day and night. Noun phrase: The brave soldiers of our army. (2) I have read 'an interesting book about the Madina Charter'. Noun phrase: an interesting book about the Madina Charter. (3) 'All the students of Class 9' took part in the debate. Noun phrase: All the students of Class 9.

Revision — Exercise 6: Change from singular to plural and from plural to singular

  • Q: i. He is a smart boy. (Change into plural.)
    Ans: They are smart boys.
  • Q: ii. Is he a nice character? (Change into plural.)
    Ans: Are they nice characters?
  • Q: iii. Is this man a worker? (Change into plural.)
    Ans: Are these men workers?
  • Q: iv. Are the bottles on the table? (Change into singular.)
    Ans: Is the bottle on the table?
  • Q: v. The pencils are not in the boxes. (Change into singular.)
    Ans: The pencil is not in the box.

Revision — Exercise 7: Rewrite the sentences by replacing the underlined words with pronouns

  • Q: i. Farid planted the cucumbers so that Farid would have the cucumber for salad. (Replace the underlined words 'Farid' and 'cucumber' with pronouns.)
    Ans: Farid planted the cucumbers so that he would have it for salad.
  • Q: ii. The children loved the parrot and taught the parrot singing. (Replace the underlined words 'the parrot' with a pronoun.)
    Ans: The children loved the parrot and taught it singing.
  • Q: iii. When the alarm rang, I turned the alarm off. (Replace the underlined words 'the alarm' with a pronoun.)
    Ans: When the alarm rang, I turned it off.
  • Q: iv. Salma washed the peaches and put the peaches in a bowl. (Replace the underlined words 'the peaches' with a pronoun.)
    Ans: Salma washed the peaches and put them in a bowl.
  • Q: v. That is the watch that Saira's parents gave Saira as graduation present. (Replace the underlined word 'Saira' with a pronoun.)
    Ans: That is the watch that Saira's parents gave her as a graduation present.

Revision — Exercise 8: Identify the pronoun antecedent

  • Q: i. Salman sent Roman the address of the house that he had bought. What is the antecedent of the pronoun 'he'?
    Ans: The antecedent of 'he' is Salman.
  • Q: ii. The first thing that Mrs. Ali reads in the newspaper is the comic strips that she loves. What is the antecedent of the pronoun 'she'?
    Ans: The antecedent of 'she' is Mrs. Ali.
  • Q: iii. When Imran and Salman came in, they were laughing. What is the antecedent of the pronoun 'they'?
    Ans: The antecedent of 'they' is Imran and Salman.
  • Q: iv. Although the tree lost several branches in the storm, it is still healthy. What is the antecedent of the pronoun 'it'?
    Ans: The antecedent of 'it' is the tree.
  • Q: v. Khanum took down the curtains but she did not have time to wash them. What is the antecedent of the pronoun 'she'?
    Ans: The antecedent of 'she' is Khanum.

Revision — Exercise 10: Fill in the blanks with the article 'a', 'an' or 'the'

  • Q: Do you live in ____ Peshawar.
    Ans: X (no article)
  • Q: He is ____ teacher who taught us English.
    Ans: the
  • Q: I bought ____ umbrella.
    Ans: an
  • Q: He has ____ lovely cat.
    Ans: a

Revision — Exercise 11: Which sentence containing a modal has the same meaning as the original one?

  • Q: i. She is not able to read Chinese. Which sentence has the same meaning?
    Options: She cannot read Chinese. / She may not read Chinese. / She need not read Chinese.
    Ans: She cannot read Chinese.
  • Q: ii. Do you think we are allowed to park here? Which sentence has the same meaning?
    Options: Do you think we may park here? / Do you think we must park here? / Do you think we need park here?
    Ans: Do you think we may park here?
  • Q: iii. You don't have to do this exercise. Which sentence has the same meaning?
    Options: You must not do this exercise. / You need not do this exercise. / You should not do this exercise.
    Ans: You need not do this exercise.
  • Q: iv. We have to stop when the traffic lights are red. Which sentence has the same meaning?
    Options: We can stop when the traffic lights are red. / We may stop when the traffic lights are red. / We must stop when the traffic lights are red.
    Ans: We must stop when the traffic lights are red.
  • Q: v. Am I allowed to ask a question? Which sentence has the same meaning?
    Options: May I ask a question? / Must I ask a question? / Should I ask a question?
    Ans: May I ask a question?

Revision — Exercise 12: Find irregular verbs from the list and use them in sentences

  • Q: Use the irregular verb 'be' in a sentence.
    Ans: She was very happy at the news of her success. (be — was/were — been)
  • Q: Use the irregular verb 'have' in a sentence.
    Ans: They had no money left at the end of the month. (have — had — had)
  • Q: Use the irregular verb 'meet' in a sentence.
    Ans: I met my old friend at the railway station yesterday. (meet — met — met)
  • Q: Use the irregular verb 'put' in a sentence.
    Ans: He put the books on the shelf. (put — put — put)
  • Q: Use the irregular verb 'buy' in a sentence.
    Ans: We bought fresh vegetables from the market. (buy — bought — bought)
  • Q: Use the irregular verb 'teach' in a sentence.
    Ans: Our teacher taught us the lesson about the Madina Charter. (teach — taught — taught)
  • Q: Use the irregular verb 'catch' in a sentence.
    Ans: The fielder caught the ball near the boundary. (catch — caught — caught)
  • Q: Use the irregular verb 'find' in a sentence.
    Ans: She found her lost keys under the table. (find — found — found)
  • Q: Use the irregular verb 'lose' in a sentence.
    Ans: Our team lost the match by two goals. (lose — lost — lost)
  • Q: Use the irregular verb 'tell' in a sentence.
    Ans: Grandmother told us an interesting story. (tell — told — told)
  • Q: Use the irregular verb 'set' in a sentence.
    Ans: The sun set behind the mountains. (set — set — set)
  • Q: Use the irregular verb 'sell' in a sentence.
    Ans: The shopkeeper sold all his goods in one day. (sell — sold — sold)
  • Q: Use the irregular verb 'build' in a sentence.
    Ans: They built a new mosque in our village last year. (build — built — built)
  • Q: Use the irregular verb 'drink' in a sentence.
    Ans: He drank a glass of cold water after the journey. (drink — drank — drunk)
  • Q: Which words in the list are not irregular verbs?
    Ans: 'Watch', 'cook', 'answer', 'want' and 'open' are regular verbs because they form their past tense by adding -ed. The word 'when' in the list is not a verb at all; it is an adverb.

Revision — Exercise 13: Find transitive verbs from the list and use them in sentences

  • Q: Use the transitive verb 'give' in a sentence.
    Ans: Please give me your notebook for a day.
  • Q: Use the transitive verb 'eat' in a sentence.
    Ans: The children eat fresh fruit every day.
  • Q: Use the transitive verb 'drink' in a sentence.
    Ans: We drink clean water to stay healthy.
  • Q: Use the transitive verb 'keep' in a sentence.
    Ans: You should keep your promise at all costs.
  • Q: Which verbs in the list (give, eat, drink, keep, go, run, look, sleep) are intransitive?
    Ans: 'Go', 'run', 'look' and 'sleep' are intransitive in their ordinary use because they do not take a direct object, for example: He goes to school; The baby is sleeping.

Revision — Exercise 14: Present participles and gerunds in 'The World of Living Things'

  • Q: Circle (identify) the present participles that are used as adjectives in the passage 'The World of Living Things'.
    Ans: The present participles used as adjectives are: 'living' (living things), 'surprising' (surprising differences), 'land-living' (land-living animals), 'flying' (flying creatures) and 'digging' (digging animals). They qualify nouns, so they work as adjectives.
  • Q: Underline (identify) the present participles that are used as gerunds in the passage 'The World of Living Things'.
    Ans: The -ing forms used as gerunds (verb-nouns) are: 'studying' (by studying how members ... are alike), 'swimming' (move from place to place by swimming), 'escaping' (burrows for escaping from predators), 'moving' (the animals' 'moving in different ways') and 'classifying' (method of classifying them; the classifying of a wider group of features).
  • Q: Double underline (identify) the gerund phrases in the passage 'The World of Living Things'.
    Ans: The gerund phrases include: 'studying how members of the animal kingdom are alike', 'escaping from predators', 'moving in different ways' and 'classifying them'. In each phrase the gerund works as a noun together with the words attached to it.

Revision — Exercise 15: Form gerunds from the verbs in the box and complete the sentences

  • Q: In many countries, ____ can provide an economical way of moving around.
    Ans: cycling
  • Q: ____ is exciting, especially if you catch a big wave.
    Ans: Surfing
  • Q: Laila is talented in ____ and has received awards in many art competitions.
    Ans: painting
  • Q: My friend's hobby is ____ so she is going to make a big cake for my birthday.
    Ans: baking
  • Q: He was accused of ____ in the examination.
    Ans: cheating
  • Q: ____ is strenuous on mountain trails.
    Ans: Hiking
  • Q: ____ is easy, but only if your rope is of the correct length.
    Ans: Skipping
  • Q: ____ is a dangerous sport.
    Ans: Racing
  • Q: Settling into a new school involves ____ new friends.
    Ans: making
  • Q: The thief admitted ____ the priceless painting.
    Ans: stealing

Revision — Exercise 16: Change the verb into correct form of present perfect tense

  • Q: She ____ (be) sick.
    Ans: has been
  • Q: I ____ (finish) my task.
    Ans: have finished
  • Q: Rashida ____ (qualify) the exam.
    Ans: has qualified
  • Q: You ____ (make) beautiful painting.
    Ans: have made
  • Q: They ____ (plan) for starting business.
    Ans: have planned

Revision — Exercise 17: Use appropriate verb form to complete the sentence in past perfect continuous tense

  • Q: She ____ (play) for two hours.
    Ans: had been playing
  • Q: They ____ (wait) for you since Wednesday.
    Ans: had been waiting
  • Q: Karim ____ (teach) since 23rd July 2007.
    Ans: had been teaching
  • Q: Haleema ____ (study) since morning.
    Ans: had been studying
  • Q: They ____ (run) their business for ten years.
    Ans: had been running

mcqs.q: She is not able to read Chinese. Which sentence has the same meaning?
options: She may not read Chinese.
She cannot read Chinese.
She need not read Chinese.
She will not read Chinese.
mcqs.why: 'Not able to' expresses lack of ability, which the modal 'cannot' also expresses, so 'She cannot read Chinese' has the same meaning.

mcqs.q: Do you think we are allowed to park here? Which sentence has the same meaning?
options: Do you think we must park here?
Do you think we need park here?
Do you think we may park here?
Do you think we shall park here?
mcqs.why: 'Allowed to' expresses permission, and 'may' is the modal of permission, so 'Do you think we may park here?' keeps the same meaning.

mcqs.q: You don't have to do this exercise. Which sentence has the same meaning?
options: You must not do this exercise.
You should not do this exercise.
You cannot do this exercise.
You need not do this exercise.
mcqs.why: 'Don't have to' means there is no necessity, which 'need not' also expresses; 'must not' would mean prohibition, a different meaning.

mcqs.q: We have to stop when the traffic lights are red. Which sentence has the same meaning?
options: We must stop when the traffic lights are red.
We can stop when the traffic lights are red.
We may stop when the traffic lights are red.
We will stop when the traffic lights are red.
mcqs.why: 'Have to' expresses obligation, and 'must' expresses the same obligation, so we must stop when the traffic lights are red.

mcqs.q: Am I allowed to ask a question? Which sentence has the same meaning?
options: Must I ask a question?
May I ask a question?
Should I ask a question?
Will I ask a question?
mcqs.why: Asking 'Am I allowed to' seeks permission, and 'May I ask a question?' is the modal form that asks for exactly that permission.

mcqs.q: Answer in the present perfect continuous tense: 'Why are you so angry? (wait, four hours)'
options: I waited for four hours.
I wait for four hours.
I have been waiting for four hours.
I had waited for four hours.
mcqs.why: The solved answer uses the present perfect continuous 'have been waiting' for an action that started in the past and explains the present anger.

mcqs.q: Make the past perfect continuous tense: 'She ____ (sleep) for ten hours when I awoke her.'
options: has been sleeping
is sleeping
was sleeping
had been sleeping
mcqs.why: Sleeping continued for ten hours before another past action, awaking her, so the past perfect continuous 'had been sleeping' is correct.

mcqs.q: Which pair correctly matches a common noun with its related proper noun?
options: city — Karachi
Karachi — city
author — book
mountain — high
mcqs.why: In the revision exercise 'city' is the common noun and 'Karachi' is its related proper noun, the name of one particular city.

mcqs.q: What is the collective noun in 'The staff quickly responded to the alarm'?
options: alarm
staff
quickly
responded
mcqs.why: 'Staff' is the collective noun because it names a whole group of people working together, treated as a single body in the sentence.

mcqs.q: What is the plural of 'brother-in-law'?
options: brother-in-laws
brothers-in-laws
brothers-in-law
brother-ins-law
mcqs.why: In compound nouns the main noun takes the plural, so 'brother-in-law' becomes 'brothers-in-law' in the revision exercise on plurals.

mcqs.q: Which of the following nouns is uncountable?
options: mango
orange
candy
sugar
mcqs.why: The revision exercise sorts 'sugar' with flour, bread, milk, tea and chocolate as uncountable, while mango, orange and candy are countable.

mcqs.q: Replace the repeated noun with a pronoun: 'Salma washed the peaches and put the peaches in a bowl.'
options: Salma washed the peaches and put them in a bowl.
Salma washed the peaches and put it in a bowl.
Salma washed the peaches and put her in a bowl.
Salma washed the peaches and put him in a bowl.
mcqs.why: 'The peaches' is plural, so it is replaced by the plural pronoun 'them': Salma washed the peaches and put them in a bowl.

mcqs.q: In 'Although the tree lost several branches in the storm, it is still healthy', what is the antecedent of 'it'?
options: the storm
the tree
several branches
the sentence
mcqs.why: The pronoun 'it' refers back to its antecedent 'the tree', which is the noun the pronoun stands for in this revision exercise.

mcqs.q: Fill in the blank with the correct article: 'I bought ____ umbrella.'
options: a
the
an
no article
mcqs.why: 'Umbrella' begins with a vowel sound, so the indefinite article 'an' is correct: I bought an umbrella, as in the revision exercise.

mcqs.q: Change into the present perfect tense: 'She ____ (be) sick.'
options: has been
have been
was been
is been
mcqs.why: With the third-person singular subject 'she', the present perfect of 'be' is 'has been': She has been sick, as in the revision exercise.

lessons.title: Writing
lessons.notes_html:
Writing A — Compare Madina Charter with the UN Human Rights Charter

  • Q: A. Compare Madina Charter with the UN Human Rights Charter.
    Ans: The Madina Charter was drafted by Hazrat Muhammad (peace be upon him) in Madina in the 7th century, while the Universal Declaration of Human Rights was adopted by the General Assembly of the United Nations in 1948. Despite the gap of about thirteen centuries, the two documents agree on the basic rights of human beings. Both declare that all people are equal citizens and that no one may be discriminated against on the basis of religion, caste or creed. The Madina Charter gave the Muslims, the Jews and other communities full freedom to profess their own religion and perform their religious ceremonies, and the UN declaration likewise proclaims the religious, personal, civic, political, economic, social and cultural rights of all human beings. Both protect the oppressed and the weak: the Charter declared bloodshed, murder and violence forbidden in Madina, while the UN declaration gives everyone the right to live in freedom and safety and says that nobody has the right to hurt or torture another. Both also make the individual, not his whole community, responsible for his own offence, and both place disputes under a just authority and a common law. The main difference is one of scope and time: the Madina Charter was a working constitution for one city-state, applied in practice from the day it was signed, whereas the UN declaration is a universal statement of thirty points for all nations. The fact that the clauses of the Madina Charter were later incorporated in the UN declaration shows that the Charter was far ahead of its time.

Writing B — Summary of the lesson 'The Madina Charter'

  • Q: B. Develop a mind map and write down the summary of the lesson 'The Madina Charter'.
    Ans: Mind map (in words): Centre — The Madina Charter and Peaceful Co-existence. Branches: (1) People of Madina — Muhajireen (Refugees), Ansar (Helpers), idol worshippers and Jews; (2) Purpose — harmony, co-operation and one common nationality; (3) Main points — collective defence, freedom of religion, individual responsibility for offences, protection of the oppressed, no bloodshed or violence, disputes referred to Hazrat Muhammad (peace be upon him); (4) Importance — civic equality, freedom of worship, religious and racial tolerance; (5) Later influence — Quaid-e-Azam's address of 1947 and the UN Universal Declaration of Human Rights, 1948. Summary: When Hazrat Muhammad (peace be upon him) migrated to Madina, the city was inhabited by different sections of people: the Muhajireen, who had left their kith and kin in Makkah and followed him, the Ansar of Madina, who had helped him through thick and thin, and other communities including idol worshippers and Jews. To create harmony and co-operation, he abolished tribal distinction, grouped the inhabitants under one general name and drafted the Madina Charter. Under the Charter, all signatory communities formed one common nationality and were bound to defend one another collectively. Every community was free to profess its own religion, an individual's offence brought no liability on his community, the oppressed were to be protected, and bloodshed, murder and violence were declared forbidden in Madina, with all disputes referred to Hazrat Muhammad (peace be upon him) for decision. The Charter thus announced the great principles of civic equality, freedom of worship and tolerance, the same principles later repeated by Quaid-e-Azam in 1947 and adopted by the United Nations in its Universal Declaration of Human Rights in 1948.

Writing C — Read the passage and answer the following questions

  • Q: I. State whether the reference in the first sentence is anaphoric or cataphoric? (First sentence: 'When the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) migrated to Medina, this city was inhabited by different sections of people.')
    Ans: The reference is anaphoric. The words 'this city' refer back to 'Medina', which has already been mentioned earlier in the same sentence. A reference that points back to something already named is called an anaphoric reference.
  • Q: II. Locate at least two transitive and two intransitive verbs (in the given passage).
    Ans: Transitive verbs: 'inhabited' (the city was inhabited by different sections of people) and 'helped' (the converts had helped the Prophet (peace be upon him)); 'abandoned' and 'followed' are also transitive. Intransitive verbs: 'migrated' (the Prophet (peace be upon him) migrated to Medina — it takes no object) and 'were known' (they were known as Ansar — no object follows).
  • Q: III. What is the main idea of the passage?
    Ans: The main idea of the passage is that when Hazrat Muhammad (peace be upon him) migrated to Madina, the city was inhabited by different groups of people. His faithful followers from Makkah were called Muhajireen or 'Refugees', while the new converts of Madina who helped him through thick and thin were called Ansar or 'Helpers'.
  • Q: IV. Identify the tense of the passage.
    Ans: The passage is mainly in the past tense. Most sentences use the simple past (migrated, was inhabited, were known), and some use the past perfect (had abandoned, had helped) for actions completed before other past actions.

mcqs.q: According to the comparison, when and where was the Madina Charter drafted, and when was the UN Declaration adopted?
options: Both were adopted by the UN in 1948
The Madina Charter in Madina in the 7th century; the UN Declaration in 1948
Both were drafted in Madina in the 7th century
The Madina Charter in 1948; the UN Declaration in the 7th century
mcqs.why: The comparison states the Madina Charter was drafted in Madina in the 7th century, while the UN Declaration was adopted in 1948.

mcqs.q: What is stated as the main difference between the two charters?
options: They disagree on every human right
The UN Declaration allows discrimination
The Madina Charter was a working constitution for one city-state, while the UN Declaration is a universal statement of thirty points for all nations
The Madina Charter had thirty points and the UN Declaration had none
mcqs.why: The comparison says the difference is scope and time: one working city-state constitution applied at once, versus a universal thirty-point statement.

mcqs.q: On what do both charters agree, according to the comparison?
options: All people are equal citizens and no one may be discriminated against on the basis of religion, caste or creed
Only rulers should enjoy rights
Religion should not be practised freely
Whole communities should pay for one person's offence
mcqs.why: Both documents declare all people equal citizens with no discrimination on the basis of religion, caste or creed, as the comparison explains.

mcqs.q: What is at the centre of the mind map developed for the summary?
options: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights only
The journey from Makkah to Madina
Quaid-e-Azam's address of 1947
The Madina Charter and Peaceful Co-existence
mcqs.why: The summary's mind map places 'The Madina Charter and Peaceful Co-existence' at the centre, with branches for people, purpose and main points.

mcqs.q: According to the summary, who helped the Prophet (peace be upon him) through thick and thin?
options: The Muhajireen from Makkah
The Ansar of Madina
The idol worshippers
The Jews of Madina
mcqs.why: The summary calls the new converts of Madina the Ansar or Helpers because they helped the Prophet through thick and thin, in all conditions.

mcqs.q: According to the summary, what happened to disputes under the Charter?
options: They were settled by each tribe alone
They were left undecided
They were referred to Hazrat Muhammad (peace be upon him) for decision
They were settled by fighting
mcqs.why: The summary lists as a main point that all disputes were referred to Hazrat Muhammad (peace be upon him) for a just decision.

mcqs.q: In Writing C, why is the reference in 'When the Prophet migrated to Medina, this city was inhabited...' called anaphoric?
options: Because 'this city' points forward to a word not yet mentioned
Because 'this city' refers back to 'Medina', already mentioned earlier in the sentence
Because the sentence has no reference at all
Because 'inhabited' is a transitive verb
mcqs.why: A reference pointing back to something already named is anaphoric; here 'this city' points back to 'Medina' mentioned earlier in the sentence.

mcqs.q: Which verb from the Writing C passage is intransitive?
options: inhabited
helped
migrated
followed
mcqs.why: Writing C identifies 'migrated' as intransitive because the Prophet migrated to Medina and the verb takes no direct object after it.

mcqs.q: What is the tense of the Writing C passage, according to the solved answer?
options: Mainly present tense throughout
Mainly future tense throughout
Only past perfect tense throughout
Mainly past tense, with simple past and some past perfect forms
mcqs.why: The passage is mainly in the past tense, using simple past forms like migrated and was inhabited, plus past perfect forms like had helped.

mcqs.q: Which later influences are named at the end of the summary?
options: Only the trade agreements of Madina
Quaid-e-Azam's address of 1947 and the UN Universal Declaration of Human Rights of 1948
The tribal customs of Makkah
The laws of other city-states only
mcqs.why: The summary ends by noting the same principles were repeated by Quaid-e-Azam in 1947 and adopted by the UN in its 1948 Declaration.

lessons.title: Practice Activities
lessons.notes_html:
Listening and Speaking

  • Q: Share with the class your point of view about peaceful co-existence. (Model response)
    Ans: In my view, peaceful co-existence means that people of different religions, languages and backgrounds live together with mutual respect, without forcing their beliefs on one another. The Madina Charter is its finest example: Muslims, Jews and other communities lived in one city, each free to follow its own religion, yet united as one nationality for defence and justice.
