Peaceful co-existence is possible only when we practise tolerance, protect the weak and settle our disputes through law instead of violence. A society built on these principles is strong, safe and prosperous for everyone.

lessons.title: Reading and Comprehension
lessons.notes_html:
Pre-Reading

  • Q: Q1. Do you like humorous stories?
    Ans: Yes, I like humorous stories very much. They make us laugh, refresh our minds and often teach a useful lesson about daily life in a light and pleasant way.
  • Q: Q2. Have you ever heard about Nasiruddin?
    Ans: Yes, I have heard about Nasiruddin. He is a famous character of folk tales whose witty anecdotes are popular all over the world. His stories are short and funny, but each one shows his quick wisdom and common sense.

Glossary

  • Q: Define 'pomp'.
    Ans: The impressive clothes, decorations, music, etc. and traditional customs that are part of an official occasion or ceremony.
  • Q: Define 'claim'.
    Ans: To say that something is true although it has not been proved and other people may not believe it.
  • Q: Define 'anecdote'.
    Ans: A short, interesting or amusing story about a real person or event.
  • Q: Define 'merchant'.
    Ans: A person who buys and sells goods in large quantities, especially one who imports and exports goods.
  • Q: Define 'cloak'.
    Ans: A type of coat that has no sleeves, fastens at the neck and hangs loosely from the shoulders, worn especially in the past.
  • Q: Define 'worn out'.
    Ans: Badly damaged and/or no longer useful because it has been used a lot.
  • Q: Define 'furious'.
    Ans: Very angry.
  • Q: Define 'turban'.
    Ans: A long piece of cloth wound tightly around the head, worn, for example, by Muslim or Sikh men.
  • Q: Define 'ornament'.
    Ans: An object that is used as decoration in a room, garden, yard, etc. rather than for a particular purpose.
  • Q: Define 'ransacking'.
    Ans: To make a place untidy, causing damage, because you are looking for something.
  • Q: Define 'fright'.
    Ans: A feeling of fear.
  • Q: Define 'gallop'.
    Ans: To move very fast and each step includes a stage when all four feet are off the ground together.
  • Q: Define 'blown'.
    Ans: To be moved by the wind.
  • Q: Define 'uproot'.
    Ans: To pull a tree, plant, etc. out of the ground.
  • Q: Define 'interrupt'.
    Ans: To say or do something that makes somebody stop what they are saying or doing.
  • Q: Define 'bray'.
    Ans: The loud unpleasant sound of a donkey.
  • Q: Define 'preference'.
    Ans: A greater interest in or desire for somebody or something than somebody or something else.

Comprehension — Questions and Answers

  • Q: Q1. What are Nasiruddin's stories famous for?
    Ans: Nasiruddin's stories are famous all over the world for their humour and wisdom. They deal with the experiences of day-to-day life, so ordinary people enjoy them and repeat them. Several volumes of his stories have been published in England, and translations have appeared in Chinese, Urdu and Pashto.
  • Q: Q2. Which anecdote from the lesson you liked the most? Why.
    Ans: I liked the anecdote of the borrowed donkey the most. Nasiruddin told his neighbour that the donkey had already been lent out, but just then the donkey brayed from the stable. Instead of feeling ashamed, Nasiruddin shut the door saying that a man who believes a donkey in preference to him does not deserve to be lent anything. I liked it because his quick, confident reply turns an embarrassing situation into laughter.
  • Q: Q3. Explain the point of laughter in the last story?
    Ans: In the last story Nasiruddin refuses to lend his donkey by telling a lie, but the donkey itself exposes the lie by braying from the stable. The laughter lies in Nasiruddin's bold reply: instead of admitting his lie, he blames the neighbour for trusting the donkey's voice more than his own words. His presence of mind and dignity in a hopeless position make the reader laugh.
  • Q: Q4. How were the thieves treated by Nasiruddin?
    Ans: Nasiruddin did not fight or shout at the thieves who entered his house. He hid himself in a cupboard, and when they opened it and asked why he was hiding, he answered politely that he was hiding because of shame. He said there was nothing in his house worthy of them, and in this witty way he treated them without anger or violence.
  • Q: Q5. What was Nasiruddin's explanation to the gardener?
    Ans: Nasiruddin was caught filling a sack with vegetables in someone's kitchen garden. He explained to the gardener that he had been blown there by the wind. He said he had caught hold of the vegetables only to stop himself being swept along, and about the vegetables in the sack he said that this was exactly what he was wondering about when the gardener interrupted him.
  • Q: Q6. Have you ever come across a humorous person like Nasiruddin? Compare the character of Nasiruddin with that real life person.
    Ans: Yes, I have come across an elderly man in our village who is humorous like Nasiruddin. Like Nasiruddin, he always has a witty answer ready and makes everyone laugh even in difficult situations. Both of them use humour to teach a lesson and to escape embarrassment cleverly. However, Nasiruddin's humour is famous all over the world, while this man's jokes are known only in our own village.
  • Q: Q7. Write a note on character of Nasiruddin using evidence from the lesson.
    Ans: Nasiruddin is a witty, wise and humorous character whose anecdotes deal with day-to-day life. He had been a tailor, a merchant, a doctor and a judge, and he had travelled widely, so he understood people well. His presence of mind is seen everywhere: he answers the farmer by putting his turban on the farmer's head, faces the thieves with a polite joke about shame, and escapes the gardener with clever excuses. He never loses his temper or his dignity, and his humour always carries common sense.

mcqs.q: What is an 'anecdote', according to the glossary?
options: A long piece of cloth wound around the head
A short, interesting or amusing story about a real person or event
A person who buys and sells goods in large quantities
An object used only as decoration in a room
mcqs.why: The glossary defines an anecdote as a short, interesting or amusing story about a real person or event, which describes Nasiruddin's tales.

mcqs.q: What are Nasiruddin's stories famous all over the world for?
options: Their length and difficult language
Their pomp and ceremony
Their humour and wisdom about day-to-day life
Their stories of kings and battles only
mcqs.why: The lesson says his stories are famous for their humour and wisdom and deal with the experiences of day-to-day life that everyone enjoys.

mcqs.q: How did Nasiruddin treat the thieves who entered his house?
options: He fought and shouted at them angrily
He hid in a cupboard and politely said he was hiding from shame as nothing in his house was worthy of them
He gave them all his money at once
He ran away and called the neighbours
mcqs.why: He did not fight or shout; he hid in a cupboard and witty-polite­ly said he hid from shame because nothing in his house was worthy of them.

mcqs.q: What was Nasiruddin's explanation to the gardener when caught with vegetables?
options: He said the gardener had given him permission
He said the sack belonged to someone else
He said he had been blown there by the wind and held the vegetables to stop himself being swept along
He said he was the owner of the garden
mcqs.why: He told the gardener he had been blown there by the wind and caught the vegetables only to stop himself being swept along by it.

mcqs.q: What is the point of laughter in the borrowed donkey story?
options: The neighbour lends his own donkey instead
Nasiruddin admits his lie at once and apologises
The donkey runs away from the stable
Nasiruddin boldly says a man who believes a donkey in preference to him does not deserve to be lent anything
mcqs.why: The laughter lies in his bold reply after the braying donkey exposed his lie: he blames the neighbour for trusting the donkey over him.

mcqs.q: What is a 'cloak', according to the glossary?
options: A type of coat with no sleeves that fastens at the neck and hangs loosely from the shoulders
A long comfortable seat for two people
A feeling of sudden fear
The loud unpleasant sound of a donkey
mcqs.why: The glossary defines a cloak as a sleeveless type of coat that fastens at the neck and hangs loosely from the shoulders, worn in the past.

mcqs.q: Which jobs had Nasiruddin held, according to the note on his character?
options: Farmer, gardener and thief
Tailor, merchant, doctor and judge
King, soldier and teacher
Merchant, farmer and gardener only
mcqs.why: The character note says he had been a tailor, a merchant, a doctor and a judge and had travelled widely, so he understood people well.

mcqs.q: What does the phrase 'worthy of you' mean in the thieves story?
options: Fit for you or deserving of you; good enough for you
Hidden from you in a cupboard
Blown towards you by the wind
Afraid of you and running away
mcqs.why: The vocabulary note explains 'worthy of you' means fit for or deserving of you, that is, good enough or valuable enough for the thieves.

mcqs.q: How did Nasiruddin answer the farmer who mocked his big turban, according to the character note?
options: He read the letter silently
He placed his turban on the farmer's head
He refused to speak to the farmer
He gave the farmer a new turban
mcqs.why: The character note cites this as presence of mind: he answers the farmer by putting his turban on the farmer's head about reading the letter.

mcqs.q: What does 'worn out' mean, as used for Jalal's cloak?
options: Moved quickly by the wind
Badly damaged and no longer useful because it has been used a lot
Used only as a decoration
Wound tightly around the head
mcqs.why: The glossary defines 'worn out' as badly damaged and no longer useful because it has been used a lot, which is why a new cloak was asked for.

lessons.title: Language Focus
lessons.notes_html:
Vocabulary B — Use the Following Words in Sentences of Your Own

  • Q: Use 'popular' in a sentence of your own.
    Ans: Nasiruddin's anecdotes are popular among people of all ages.
  • Q: Use 'worn out' in a sentence of your own.
    Ans: Jalal asked for a cloak because his own cloak was worn out.
  • Q: Use 'turban' in a sentence of your own.
    Ans: The old man wore a big white turban on his head.
  • Q: Use 'gallop' in a sentence of your own.
    Ans: The frightened horse began to gallop down the road.
  • Q: Use 'blown' in a sentence of your own.
    Ans: The dry leaves were blown from one corner of the street to the other.
  • Q: Use 'ornament' in a sentence of your own.
    Ans: She bought a gold ornament with her savings.

Vocabulary A — What Do You Understand by the Following Terms from the Lesson?

  • Q: Give the meaning of the phrase 'worthy of you'.
    Ans: It means fit for you or deserving of you. In the story Nasiruddin tells the thieves that there is nothing in his house worthy of you, that is, nothing good enough or valuable enough for them to steal.
  • Q: Give the meaning of the phrase 'to get money not advice'.
    Ans: It means that the person has come to obtain money, not to listen to advice. Nasiruddin says this to the rich man who, instead of giving him money to buy an elephant, starts advising him that he cannot afford to keep an elephant.
  • Q: Give the meaning of the phrase 'being swept along'.
    Ans: It means being carried away by force, here being carried away by the strong wind. Nasiruddin tells the gardener that he held the vegetables to stop himself being swept along by the wind.
  • Q: Give the meaning of the phrase 'experiences of day-to-day life'.
    Ans: It means the ordinary events, happenings and experiences of everyday life. Nasiruddin's stories are popular because they are about such common daily experiences that everyone can understand and enjoy.

Grammar A — Complete the Sentences Using an Adjective of the Category Specified

  • Q: We had to take a ____ route to reach our destination. (Adjective of quality)
    Ans: short
  • Q: We should be ____ citizens. (Adjective of quality)
    Ans: good
  • Q: He is wearing ____ suit. (Adjective of colour)
    Ans: red
  • Q: Burj Al-Khalifa is the ____ building in the world. (Adjective of size)
    Ans: tallest
  • Q: The earth is ____. (Adjective of shape)
    Ans: round

Grammar B — Complete the Sentences Using the Appropriate Degree of the Adjective in Brackets

  • Q: He is ____ than his neighbors. (rich)
    Ans: richer
  • Q: The brides were much ____ than the grooms. (young)
    Ans: younger
  • Q: He is ____ student of the class. (intelligent)
    Ans: the most intelligent
  • Q: He is ____ than I thought him to be. (clever)
    Ans: cleverer
  • Q: When the old woman became ____ she began to move about. (strong)
    Ans: stronger

Grammar C — Complete the Sentences Using Proper Order of Adjective

  • Q: Q1. He was wearing a ____ shirt.
    Options: dirty old flannel / flannel old dirty / old dirty flannel
    Ans: dirty old flannel
  • Q: Q2. Pass me the ____ cups.
    Options: plastic big blue / big blue plastic / big plastic blue
    Ans: big blue plastic
  • Q: Q3. He sat behind a ____ desk.
    Options: big wooden brown / big brown wooden / wooden big brown
    Ans: big brown wooden
  • Q: Q4. I used to drive ____ car.
    Options: a blue old German / an old German blue / an old blue German
    Ans: an old blue German
  • Q: Q5. She gave him a ____ vase.
    Options: small Egyptian black / black Egyptian small / small black Egyptian
    Ans: small black Egyptian

Grammar D — Formation of Adjectives: Use the Word in Brackets to Form a Suitable Adjective

  • Q: Hameed writes in a simple and ____ way. (understand)
    Ans: understandable
  • Q: The party was much more ____ than I had expected. (enjoy)
    Ans: enjoyable
  • Q: I wish I had ____ powers. (magic)
    Ans: magical
  • Q: Maria came to me in a very ____ state. (emotion)
    Ans: emotional
  • Q: My sister is ____ to cats. (allergy)
    Ans: allergic

Grammar E — Find Adjectives from the Lesson and Change Them into Comparative and Superlative Degrees

  • Q: Give the comparative and superlative degrees of 'great'.
    Ans: Comparative: greater. Superlative: greatest.
  • Q: Give the comparative and superlative degrees of 'big'.
    Ans: Comparative: bigger. Superlative: biggest.
  • Q: Give the comparative and superlative degrees of 'funny'.
    Ans: Comparative: funnier. Superlative: funniest.
  • Q: Give the comparative and superlative degrees of 'fine'.
    Ans: Comparative: finer. Superlative: finest.
  • Q: Give the comparative and superlative degrees of 'old'.
    Ans: Comparative: older. Superlative: oldest.
  • Q: Give the comparative and superlative degrees of 'large'.
    Ans: Comparative: larger. Superlative: largest.

Grammar F — Identify the Adjective Phrases in the Following Sentences

  • Q: Q1. Identify the adjective phrase: Have you ever seen an elephant with a white skin?
    Ans: The adjective phrase is 'with a white skin'. It modifies the noun 'elephant'.
  • Q: Q2. Identify the adjective phrase: He was wearing a crown made of gold.
    Ans: The adjective phrase is 'made of gold'. It modifies the noun 'crown'.
  • Q: Q3. Identify the adjective phrase: There I met a girl with blue eyes.
    Ans: The adjective phrase is 'with blue eyes'. It modifies the noun 'girl'.
  • Q: Q4. Identify the adjective phrase: Wild beasts in small cages are a sorry sight.
    Ans: The adjective phrase is 'in small cages'. It modifies the noun 'beasts'.
  • Q: Q5. Identify the adjective phrase: A man with a long beard came to see me.
    Ans: The adjective phrase is 'with a long beard'. It modifies the noun 'man'.

Grammar G — Replace the Adjective by an Adjective Phrase of the Same Meaning

  • Q: Q1. Replace the adjective with an adjective phrase: It is a white elephant.
    Ans: It is an elephant with a white skin.
  • Q: Q2. Replace the adjective with an adjective phrase: He lived in a stone house.
    Ans: He lived in a house made of stone.
  • Q: Q3. Replace the adjective with an adjective phrase: The king wore golden crown.
    Ans: The king wore a crown made of gold.
  • Q: Q4. Replace the adjective with an adjective phrase: She wore a diamond necklace.
    Ans: She wore a necklace made of diamond.
  • Q: Q5. Replace the adjective with an adjective phrase: It was horrible night.
    Ans: It was a night of horror.

mcqs.q: He was wearing a ____ shirt.
options: flannel old dirty
old dirty flannel
dirty old flannel
flannel dirty old
mcqs.why: Adjectives follow the order opinion or quality before age before material, so 'dirty old flannel' is the correct order for the shirt.

mcqs.q: Pass me the ____ cups.
options: plastic big blue
big plastic blue
blue plastic big
big blue plastic
mcqs.why: The correct order is size before colour before material, giving 'big blue plastic' cups, as in the solved Grammar C exercise.

mcqs.q: He sat behind a ____ desk.
options: big brown wooden
big wooden brown
wooden big brown
brown big wooden
mcqs.why: Size comes before colour and colour before material, so the desk is correctly described as a 'big brown wooden' desk.

mcqs.q: I used to drive ____ car.
options: a blue old German
an old German blue
an old blue German
an blue old German
mcqs.why: Age comes before colour and colour before origin, so the correct order with the right article is 'an old blue German' car.

mcqs.q: She gave him a ____ vase.
options: small Egyptian black
black Egyptian small
small black Egyptian
Egyptian small black
mcqs.why: Size comes before colour and colour before origin, so the vase is correctly described as a 'small black Egyptian' vase.

mcqs.q: What does the phrase 'to get money not advice' mean in the lesson?
options: The person has come to obtain money, not to listen to advice
The person has come to give money and advice
The person wants neither money nor advice
The person has come to sell an elephant
mcqs.why: Nasiruddin says this to the rich man who, instead of giving money for an elephant, starts advising him, so he came for money, not advice.

mcqs.q: What does 'being swept along' mean in Nasiruddin's excuse to the gardener?
options: Being hidden inside a cupboard
Being carried away by force, here by the strong wind
Being decorated like an ornament
Being stopped by an interruption
mcqs.why: The phrase means being carried away by force; Nasiruddin claims he held the vegetables to stop himself being swept along by the wind.

mcqs.q: Which adjective in the Grammar A examples is an adjective of shape, in 'The earth is ____'?
options: short
red
round
tallest
mcqs.why: The solved example completes 'The earth is round', and 'round' describes shape, unlike 'short' for quality or 'red' for colour.

mcqs.q: Complete with the correct degree: 'He is ____ than his neighbors. (rich)'
options: rich
richer
richest
the most rich
mcqs.why: The word 'than' requires the comparative degree, so 'rich' becomes 'richer': He is richer than his neighbors, as in Grammar B.

mcqs.q: Complete with the correct degree: 'He is ____ student of the class. (intelligent)'
options: intelligent
more intelligent
the most intelligent
intelligenter
mcqs.why: Comparison with the whole class requires the superlative with 'the', so he is 'the most intelligent' student of the class.

mcqs.q: Form a suitable adjective from 'enjoy': 'The party was much more ____ than I had expected.'
options: enjoyment
enjoyable
enjoyed
enjoying
mcqs.why: The adjective formed from 'enjoy' is 'enjoyable' with the suffix -able, which correctly describes how pleasant the party was.

mcqs.q: Form a suitable adjective from 'allergy': 'My sister is ____ to cats.'
options: allergy
allergies
allergic
allergen
mcqs.why: The adjective formed from 'allergy' is 'allergic', so the solved sentence reads: My sister is allergic to cats.

mcqs.q: What are the comparative and superlative degrees of 'funny'?
options: funnyer and funnyest
more funny and most funny
funnier and funniest
funniest and funnier
mcqs.why: Grammar E gives 'funny' with comparative 'funnier' and superlative 'funniest', changing the final y to i before adding -er and -est.

mcqs.q: What is the adjective phrase in 'Have you ever seen an elephant with a white skin'?
options: Have you ever seen
an elephant
with a white skin
ever seen an elephant
mcqs.why: Grammar F identifies 'with a white skin' as the adjective phrase because it modifies and describes the noun 'elephant' in the sentence.

mcqs.q: Replace the adjective with an adjective phrase: 'He lived in a stone house.'
options: He lived in a house of horror.
He lived in a house made of stone.
He lived in a stony house.
He lived in a house with a long beard.
mcqs.why: Grammar G replaces 'stone' with the phrase 'made of stone', giving 'He lived in a house made of stone' with the same meaning.

lessons.title: Writing
lessons.notes_html:
Writing — How to Write a Book Review?

  • Q: Q1. How to write a book review?
    Ans: A book review gives the reader a clear idea of a book and the reviewer's opinion about it. It should include the title of the book, its type and style, the main idea, the important characters, whether you liked it or not and why, and a suitable ending or conclusion. These points can first be arranged in a mind map, as shown in the lesson, and then written in connected paragraphs.

Writing A — Write a Review of the Lesson Nasiruddin

  • Q: Q1. Write a review of the lesson Nasiruddin.
    Ans: The lesson 'Nasiruddin' is a collection of humorous anecdotes about the famous folk character Nasiruddin, whose stories are known all over the world. Its main idea is that wit and common sense can solve the problems of day-to-day life in a pleasant way. The style is simple, light and amusing, and the language is easy for students. The main character is Nasiruddin himself, who appears as a tailor, merchant, doctor and judge, while Jalal, the farmer, the gardener and the thieves appear in different stories. I liked the lesson very much, especially the stories of the cloak, the turban and the borrowed donkey, because every story made me laugh and also taught me something. In the end, I would recommend this lesson to every reader who enjoys humour with wisdom.

Writing B — Translate the Following Passage from English to Urdu

  • Q: Q1. Translate the following passage from English to Urdu: 'A farmer brought a letter to Nasiruddin and requested him to read it for him. Nasiruddin wanted to be excused saying that he could not do so because he was illiterate. The farmer said, You are wearing such a big turban and still cannot read a letter. Nasiruddin placed his turban on the head of the farmer and said, Now you have the turban on your head. Read the letter.'
    Ans: Note: This exercise requires translation into Urdu; translations are not reproduced in these English-only solved notes.

mcqs.q: What should a book review include, according to the lesson?
options: Only the price and page count of the book
The title, type and style, main idea, important characters, whether you liked it and why, and a suitable conclusion
Only a translation of the book
Only the names of the publisher and printer
mcqs.why: The lesson says a review should include the title, type and style, main idea, important characters, your liking with reasons, and a conclusion.

mcqs.q: How should the points of a book review first be arranged, according to the lesson?
options: In a mind map, and then written in connected paragraphs
In a long list of quotations only
In a table of prices
In separate letters to the author
mcqs.why: The lesson explains that the review points can first be arranged in a mind map and then written out in connected paragraphs.

mcqs.q: What is the main idea of the lesson 'Nasiruddin', according to the review?
options: Wit and common sense can solve the problems of day-to-day life in a pleasant way
A donkey is more truthful than a man
Gardens should be guarded at all times
Travelling makes a man rich
mcqs.why: The review states the main idea is that wit and common sense can solve the problems of day-to-day life in a pleasant way.

mcqs.q: How does the review describe the style and language of the lesson?
options: Difficult, formal and boring
Simple, light and amusing, with language easy for students
Poetic and full of difficult words
Sad and frightening throughout
mcqs.why: The review describes the style as simple, light and amusing and the language as easy for students to follow and enjoy.

mcqs.q: Who is the main character in the review of the lesson?
options: Jalal
The farmer
Nasiruddin himself
The gardener
mcqs.why: The review names Nasiruddin himself as the main character, appearing as tailor, merchant, doctor and judge in the different stories.

mcqs.q: Which other characters does the review mention as appearing in different stories?
options: Only the rich man with the elephant
Jalal, the farmer, the gardener and the thieves
The king and his soldiers
No other characters at all
mcqs.why: The review lists Jalal, the farmer, the gardener and the thieves as the other characters appearing in the different anecdotes.

mcqs.q: Which stories does the reviewer say he especially liked?
options: The stories of the cloak, the turban and the borrowed donkey
The stories of the elephant only
The stories of the garden only
No story is named in the review
mcqs.why: The reviewer says he especially liked the stories of the cloak, the turban and the borrowed donkey in the lesson 'Nasiruddin'.

mcqs.q: Why did the reviewer like the lesson, according to the review?
options: Because it is the longest lesson in the book
Because every story made him laugh and also taught him something
Because it has no characters to remember
Because it is written in difficult language
mcqs.why: The reviewer liked it because every story made him laugh and also taught him something, combining humour with a useful lesson.

mcqs.q: How does the review end, in its recommendation?
options: It advises readers to avoid humorous stories
It says the lesson is only for teachers
It recommends the lesson to every reader who enjoys humour with wisdom
It asks readers to translate the lesson
mcqs.why: The review concludes by recommending the lesson to every reader who enjoys humour with wisdom, which sums up its appeal.

mcqs.q: What does a book review give the reader, according to the lesson?
options: A clear idea of a book and the reviewer's opinion about it
A complete copy of the book
Only the summary without any opinion
A list of books by the same publisher
mcqs.why: The lesson defines a book review as giving the reader a clear idea of a book together with the reviewer's own opinion about it.

lessons.title: Practice Activities
lessons.notes_html:
Listening and Speaking — Role Play

  • Q: Listening and Speaking — Role play: In a group of two carry out an interview in which the interviewer asks questions about the lesson from reviewer.
    Ans: This is an oral classroom activity with no written answer.

lessons.title: Reading and Comprehension
lessons.notes_html:
Pre-Reading

  • Q: Q1. Look at the picture and predict what the lesson is about?
    Ans: The picture shows an old stone well, so the lesson is probably about a well and the people who needed its water. From the title 'The Two Bargains', it seems the lesson will tell how the well was bought and sold, and what bargain was made for it.

Glossary

  • Q: Define 'bitter'.
    Ans: Making you feel very unhappy; caused by great unhappiness.
  • Q: Define 'broke out'.
    Ans: To start suddenly.
  • Q: Define 'decline'.
    Ans: To say that you will not do something that somebody has asked you to do.
  • Q: Define 'famine'.
    Ans: A lack of food during a long period of time in a region.
  • Q: Define 'generosity'.
    Ans: Willing to give somebody money, gifts, time or kindness freely.
  • Q: Define 'proclaim'.
    Ans: To publicly and officially tell people about something important.
  • Q: Define 'scarce'.
    Ans: There is not enough of it and it is only available in small quantities.
  • Q: Define 'touch'.
    Ans: Feeling happy and grateful because of something kind that somebody has done; feeling emotional about something.
  • Q: Define 'turn down'.
    Ans: To reject or refuse to consider an offer, a proposal, etc. or the person who makes it.
  • Q: Define 'apprise'.
    Ans: To tell or inform somebody of something.
  • Q: Define 'endowment'.
    Ans: To give or bequeath an income or property to a person or institution.

Comprehension — Questions and Answers

  • Q: Q1. Why did Hazrat Umar (RA) weep?
    Ans: Hazrat Umar (RA) wept because he was deeply touched by the generosity of Hazrat Usman (RA). He had called Hazrat Usman (RA) hard hearted for refusing his offers, but then he learnt that the flour had already been sold to Allah for a far greater reward. He wept, embraced Hazrat Usman (RA) and begged forgiveness for his harsh words.
  • Q: Q2. Why did the Jew agree to Hazrat Usman's (RA) offer?
    Ans: The Jew did not agree to sell the well at first. Then he thought it would be more profitable to make Hazrat Usman (RA) a partner, because Hazrat Usman (RA) was a rich businessman. So he agreed to sell half of his share in the well to Hazrat Usman (RA) for twelve thousand dirhams.
  • Q: Q3. What simple steps can you incorporate into your life to foster generosity?
    Ans: We can foster generosity by small and regular steps. We can share our food, books, money, time and energy with needy people, save a little in order to be able to give, and be kind and encouraging to others. We should help others without expecting anything in return, just to make their lives easier and pleasant.
  • Q: Q4. How did the Jew learn a bitter lesson?
    Ans: The Jew hoped to make more money by making Hazrat Usman (RA) a partner in the well. But Hazrat Usman (RA) allowed everyone to take water free of cost on his day, and people carried enough water to last for the next day as well. As a result the Jew earned nothing at all on his own day and was forced to offer the other half of the well for sale, and this was the bitter lesson he learnt.
  • Q: Q5. What is the role of generosity in Islamic history?
    Ans: Generosity has a great role in Islamic history, as this lesson shows. Hazrat Usman (RA) bought Bair-e-Roma and gave its water free to the people of Madina, and during the famine he gave away a thousand camel-loads of flour. Such acts ended the hardships of the people, spread love and brotherhood, and are remembered with respect to this day.
  • Q: Q6. Service to humanity is liked by Allah. Elaborate.
    Ans: Service to humanity is liked by Allah because He rewards it many times over. Hazrat Usman (RA) refused even nine times the price of the flour because Allah, his real buyer, had promised him at least ten times, and up to seventy or seven hundred times, as profit. Helping the poor and needy in times of difficulty, like famine, is therefore one of the best ways to please Allah.
  • Q: Q7. What did Hazrat Usman (RA) do when the Holy Prophet (PBUH) said, 'Is there anyone here who would like to purchase paradise for himself in return for Bair-e-Roma?'
    Ans: Hazrat Usman (RA) stood up and went out quietly without saying anything. He went straight to the Jew who owned Bair-e-Roma and offered to buy the well from him. After bargaining, he bought half of the share in the well for twelve thousand dirhams and then offered his share to the Holy Prophet (PBUH) for the people.
  • Q: Q8. Why did Hazrat Usman (RA) keep on rejecting the offer of Hazrat Umar (RA)?
    Ans: Hazrat Usman (RA) kept on rejecting the offers of Hazrat Umar (RA) because he had already sold his stock of flour to another buyer. That buyer was Allah, who had promised him at least ten times the price as profit, and possibly seventy or even seven hundred times. No offer of Hazrat Umar (RA), even nine times the price, could match that reward.
  • Q: Q9. Identify a real life situation / problem that could be improved with generosity and how will you display personal generosity to that situation / problem?
    Ans: A real life problem that can be improved with generosity is the difficulty of poor students who cannot buy books, uniforms and school bags. I can display personal generosity by sharing my own books, giving my saved pocket money, and collecting used books and clothes from my class for them. I can also give my time to help weak students in their studies without expecting anything in return.

Comprehension B — Choose the Correct Answer

  • Q: Q1. When the Holy Prophet (PBUH) said, 'Is there anyone here who would like to purchase paradise for himself in return for Baire Roma?' Hazrat Usman (RA) stood up and went out quietly to ____.
    Options: ask the owner of Bair-e-Roma to give people water / make a bargain with the owner of the well / avoid the question asked by Holy Prophet (PBUH) / talk with the people about the problem they were facing
    Ans: make a bargain with the owner of the well
  • Q: Q2. Hazrat Usman (RA) turned down Hazrat Umar's (RA) offer and said, 'I have another buyer who is offering me much more'. The other buyer was offering ____.
    Options: nine times the price of the flour / 25 times the price of the flour / ten times, seventy times or even seven hundred times the price of the flour / three times the price of the flour
    Ans: ten times, seventy times or even seven hundred times the price of the flour
  • Q: Q3. The people could not get water from Bair-e-Roma because ____.
    Options: it was not always suitable for drinking / they had to travel long distances to fetch water / it was owned by a Jew who sold its water at a high price / the water was very sweet
    Ans: it was owned by a Jew who sold its water at a high price
  • Q: Q4. How was the food distributed among the people of Madina?
    Options: it was distributed among the people happily and generously / it was distributed among the people with high price / it was distributed among the people sadly and charitably / it was distributed among the people stingily
    Ans: it was distributed among the people happily and generously
  • Q: Q5. It was proclaimed in Medina that ____ on the day the well belonged to Hazrat Usman (RA).
    Options: Muslims could carry, free of cost, as much water as they liked / everyone could carry as much water as he liked free of cost / everyone could carry water after payment of certain cost / Muslims could carry limited amount of water free of cost
    Ans: everyone could carry as much water as he liked free of cost

mcqs.q: When the Holy Prophet (PBUH) said, 'Is there anyone here who would like to purchase paradise for himself in return for Baire Roma?' Hazrat Usman (RA) stood up and went out quietly to ____.
options: ask the owner of Bair-e-Roma to give people water
avoid the question asked by Holy Prophet (PBUH)
make a bargain with the owner of the well
talk with the people about the problem they were facing
mcqs.why: Hazrat Usman (RA) went straight to the Jew who owned Bair-e-Roma and offered to buy the well from him, so he went out to make a bargain with its owner.

mcqs.q: Hazrat Usman (RA) turned down Hazrat Umar's (RA) offer and said, 'I have another buyer who is offering me much more'. The other buyer was offering ____.
options: ten times, seventy times or even seven hundred times the price of the flour
nine times the price of the flour
25 times the price of the flour
three times the price of the flour
mcqs.why: The other buyer was Allah, who had promised Hazrat Usman (RA) at least ten times the price, and possibly seventy or even seven hundred times, as his reward.

mcqs.q: The people could not get water from Bair-e-Roma because ____.
options: it was not always suitable for drinking
they had to travel long distances to fetch water
the water was very sweet
it was owned by a Jew who sold its water at a high price
mcqs.why: Bair-e-Roma was the only well of sweet water in Madina, but its Jewish owner sold its water at a high price, so the poor companions found it hard to get water.

mcqs.q: How was the food distributed among the people of Madina?
options: it was distributed among the people with high price
it was distributed among the people happily and generously
it was distributed among the people sadly and charitably
it was distributed among the people stingily
mcqs.why: After Hazrat Usman (RA) refused every worldly offer for his flour, the thousand camel-loads were distributed among the people of Madina happily and generously.

mcqs.q: It was proclaimed in Medina that ____ on the day the well belonged to Hazrat Usman (RA).
options: Muslims could carry, free of cost, as much water as they liked
everyone could carry water after payment of certain cost
everyone could carry as much water as he liked free of cost
Muslims could carry limited amount of water free of cost
mcqs.why: The proclamation was for everyone, not only for Muslims, and it allowed each person to carry as much water as he liked completely free of cost on Hazrat Usman's (RA) day.

mcqs.q: Why did Hazrat Umar (RA) weep after his argument with Hazrat Usman (RA)?
options: He was angry that the flour had been sold to someone else
He had lost the bargain for the well of Bair-e-Roma
He was deeply touched by Hazrat Usman's (RA) generosity and begged forgiveness for his harsh words
He feared that the famine in Madina would never end
mcqs.why: Hazrat Umar (RA) wept because he was deeply touched when he learnt the flour had already been sold to Allah; he embraced Hazrat Usman (RA) and begged forgiveness for calling him hard hearted.

mcqs.q: For how much did Hazrat Usman (RA) buy half of the share in Bair-e-Roma?
options: Nine thousand dirhams
Twelve thousand dirhams
Ten thousand dirhams
Seven hundred dirhams
mcqs.why: After bargaining with the Jew, Hazrat Usman (RA) bought half of the share in the well for twelve thousand dirhams and offered that share for the people of Madina.

mcqs.q: Why did the Jew at first agree to make Hazrat Usman (RA) a partner in the well?
options: He wanted to give the well away as an endowment
He was afraid of the people of Madina
He wanted the well to be free for everyone
He thought it would be more profitable because Hazrat Usman (RA) was a rich businessman
mcqs.why: The Jew refused to sell the whole well at first, but he agreed to sell half his share because he thought partnership with a rich businessman like Hazrat Usman (RA) would be more profitable.

mcqs.q: How did the Jew learn a bitter lesson from his bargain?
options: People stored free water on Hazrat Usman's (RA) day for the next day too, so he earned nothing on his own day
Hazrat Usman (RA) refused to pay him the agreed price for the well
The water of the well suddenly turned bitter and undrinkable
The people of Madina stopped coming to the well altogether
mcqs.why: On Hazrat Usman's (RA) day everyone took water free and carried enough to last the next day as well, so the Jew earned nothing on his own day and was forced to sell the other half.

mcqs.q: What reached Madina during the famine in the days of Caliph Umar (RA)?
options: A thousand camel-loads of flour belonging to Hazrat Usman (RA)
A caravan carrying a thousand new wells for Madina
Nine hundred camel-loads of dates for the market
A ship carrying flour bought by Hazrat Umar (RA)
mcqs.why: During the famine, a thousand camel-loads of flour belonging to Hazrat Usman (RA) reached Madina, and this flour became the subject of the second bargain in the lesson.

lessons.title: Language Focus
lessons.notes_html:
Vocabulary A — Look Up the Meanings in the Dictionary and Make Sentences

  • Q: Q1. Explain the difference between 'fetch' and 'bring', with sentences to bring out the meaning.
    Ans: 'Fetch' means to go to a place, get something and bring it back; for example, go and fetch water from the well. 'Bring' means to carry or take something to a person or place; for example, bring me a glass of water. The difference is that fetch includes going and returning, while bring only means carrying towards someone.
  • Q: Q2. Explain the difference between 'famous' and 'notorious', with sentences to bring out the meaning.
    Ans: 'Famous' means well known for a good reason; for example, Hazrat Usman (RA) is famous for his generosity. 'Notorious' means well known for a bad reason; for example, the thief was notorious in the whole town. Both words mean widely known, but famous has a good sense and notorious has a bad sense.
  • Q: Q3. Explain the difference between 'crime' and 'sin', with sentences to bring out the meaning.
    Ans: A 'crime' is a wrong act against the law of the land, such as theft, and it is punished by the state; for example, stealing is a crime. A 'sin' is a wrong act against the commands of Allah and religion, such as telling a lie, and a person is answerable to Allah for it. Some acts, like theft, are both a crime and a sin.
  • Q: Q4. Explain the difference between 'desert' and 'barren', with sentences to bring out the meaning.
    Ans: A 'desert' is a large area of dry, sandy land where very little rain falls and few plants grow; for example, Arabia is a desert land. 'Barren' describes land that cannot produce crops or plants; for example, nothing grows in that barren field. A desert is a place, while barren is a quality of land anywhere.

Vocabulary B — Write the Contextual Meanings of the Following Words

  • Q: Give the contextual meaning of 'well'.
    Ans: In this lesson 'well' means a deep hole in the ground from which water is taken out, that is, Bair-e-Roma, the well of sweet water in Madina.
  • Q: Give the contextual meaning of 'calmly'.
    Ans: In this lesson 'calmly' means quietly and peacefully, without anger or excitement, as Hazrat Usman (RA) stood up calmly and explained his bargain.
  • Q: Give the contextual meaning of 'embraced'.
    Ans: In this lesson 'embraced' means held someone tightly in the arms to show love and affection, as Hazrat Umar (RA) embraced Hazrat Usman (RA).
  • Q: Give the contextual meaning of 'begged'.
    Ans: In this lesson 'begged' means asked earnestly and humbly, as Hazrat Umar (RA) begged forgiveness for his harsh words.
  • Q: Give the contextual meaning of 'load'.
    Ans: In this lesson 'load' means the amount that is carried at one time, as in a thousand camel-load of flour, meaning the flour that a thousand camels could carry.
  • Q: Give the contextual meaning of 'profitable'.
    Ans: In this lesson 'profitable' means giving benefit or advantage, as the Jew thought it more profitable to make Hazrat Usman (RA) a partner in the well.

Grammar A — Fill in the Blanks with Suitable Adverbs from the Box

  • Q: I ____ go to bed at 10 o'clock.
    Ans: usually
  • Q: I have ____ been to the China.
    Ans: never
  • Q: I have been to Mardan just ____.
    Ans: once
  • Q: I ____ take a bath before I go to bed.
    Ans: mostly
  • Q: My grandparents live in Karachi. I visit them ____.
    Ans: occasionally
  • Q: My friends are ____ helpful.
    Ans: very
  • Q: I was ____ impressed with her performance.
    Ans: always
  • Q: I ____ go for a walk in the park.
    Ans: sometimes
  • Q: I read English novels ____.
    Ans: rarely
  • Q: They ____ go out.
    Ans: often

Grammar B — Rewrite the Sentences, Adding the Adverb in the Correct Place

  • Q: Q1. Rewrite the sentence adding the adverb in the correct place: She is at home. (rarely)
    Ans: She is rarely at home.
  • Q: Q2. Rewrite the sentence adding the adverb in the correct place: He opened the door. (quietly)
    Ans: He opened the door quietly.
  • Q: Q3. Rewrite the sentence adding the adverb in the correct place: Can I sit down? (here)
    Ans: Can I sit down here?
  • Q: Q4. Rewrite the sentence adding the adverb in the correct place: The students listened. (attentively)
    Ans: The students listened attentively.
  • Q: Q5. Rewrite the sentence adding the adverb in the correct place: We live in Abbottabad. (now)
    Ans: We now live in Abbottabad.

Grammar C — Complete Each Sentence with the Correct Form of the Adverb in Parentheses

  • Q: Our father arrived ____ than the rest of the family. (late)
    Ans: later
  • Q: My sister looked ____ than Amara did. (beautifully)
    Ans: more beautifully
  • Q: Your husband, Kamal, writes ____ of all. (well)
    Ans: best
  • Q: Mrs. Haseeb speaks ____ than Mrs. Amir. (clearly)
    Ans: more clearly
  • Q: Mother prepares chicken ____ than grandmother does. (well)
    Ans: better

Grammar D — Underline the Adverbial Phrase and Write the Question It Answers

  • Q: Q1. Underline the adverbial phrase and write the question it answers: We expect our grandparents to arrive in about an hour.
    Ans: The adverbial phrase is 'in about an hour'. It answers the question 'When?'
  • Q: Q2. Underline the adverbial phrase and write the question it answers: My cousin watches television almost as much as you do.
    Ans: The adverbial phrase is 'almost as much as you do'. It answers the question 'How much?'
  • Q: Q3. Underline the adverbial phrase and write the question it answers: The weatherman says it will rain all day.
    Ans: The adverbial phrase is 'all day'. It answers the question 'When?'
  • Q: Q4. Underline the adverbial phrase and write the question it answers: Your brother plays soccer better than my brother does.
    Ans: The adverbial phrase is 'better than my brother does'. It answers the question 'How?'
  • Q: Q5. Underline the adverbial phrase and write the question it answers: Our friend drives on Mondays.
    Ans: The adverbial phrase is 'on Mondays'. It answers the question 'When?'

Grammar E — Underline the Adverb Clause in Each Sentence

  • Q: Q1. Underline the adverb clause: Because no one was home, the thieves robbed the house.
    Ans: The adverb clause is 'Because no one was home'.
  • Q: Q2. Underline the adverb clause: If Basheer calls, please tell him I am on my way.
    Ans: The adverb clause is 'If Basheer calls'.
  • Q: Q3. Underline the adverb clause: Palwasha climbed the stairs after she finished her dinner.
    Ans: The adverb clause is 'after she finished her dinner'.
  • Q: Q4. Underline the adverb clause: He takes exercises before he goes to school.
    Ans: The adverb clause is 'before he goes to school'.
  • Q: Q5. Underline the adverb clause: You should visit the monument before you leave town.
    Ans: The adverb clause is 'before you leave town'.
  • Q: Q6. Underline the adverb clause: He takes exercises before he goes to school.
    Ans: The adverb clause is 'before he goes to school'. This sentence is printed again in the book as item 6, exactly the same as item 4.

mcqs.q: What does 'fetch' mean, as explained in the vocabulary exercise?
options: To carry something towards a person or place only
To go to a place, get something and bring it back
To be well known for a bad reason
To refuse an offer that somebody makes
mcqs.why: 'Fetch' includes both going and returning: you go to a place, get the thing, and bring it back, as in going to fetch water from the well.

mcqs.q: Which sentence uses 'bring' correctly for carrying something towards someone?
options: Go and bring water from the well and return with it
Bring me a glass of water
Fetch me to the well every morning
Bring is only used for going away from a person
mcqs.why: 'Bring' means to carry or take something to a person or place, so 'Bring me a glass of water' is correct; going and returning would need 'fetch'.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between 'famous' and 'notorious'?
options: Both words always have a bad sense
'Famous' means known for a good reason, while 'notorious' means known for a bad reason
'Notorious' means known for a good reason, while 'famous' means unknown
There is no difference between the two words at all
mcqs.why: Both words mean widely known, but 'famous' has a good sense, as Hazrat Usman (RA) is famous for generosity, while 'notorious' has a bad sense, as a thief is notorious.

mcqs.q: Which act is a 'crime', as explained in the lesson?
options: Telling a lie, which is answerable only to Allah
Stealing, a wrong act against the law of the land punished by the state
Feeling unhappy because of great sorrow
Refusing an offer made by somebody
mcqs.why: A crime is a wrong act against the law of the land, such as theft, and it is punished by the state, whereas a sin is a wrong act against the commands of Allah.

mcqs.q: What is a 'sin', according to the vocabulary exercise?
options: A wrong act against the commands of Allah and religion, for which a person is answerable to Allah
A large area of dry sandy land with very little rain
A wrong act punished only by the state courts
The amount that is carried at one time
mcqs.why: A sin is a wrong act against the commands of Allah and religion, such as telling a lie, and a person is answerable to Allah for it; some acts like theft are both a crime and a sin.

mcqs.q: How is 'barren' different from 'desert'?
options: 'Barren' is a place, while 'desert' is only a quality
A 'desert' is a place of dry sandy land, while 'barren' is a quality of land that cannot produce crops
'Barren' means land full of crops and plants
'Desert' means land that always produces rich crops
mcqs.why: A desert is a place: a large area of dry, sandy land with very little rain. Barren is a quality of land anywhere that cannot produce crops or plants, as in a barren field.

mcqs.q: In this lesson, what does the word 'well' mean in context?
options: A deep hole in the ground from which water is taken out
A feeling of happiness and gratitude
The amount carried by a camel at one time
A public announcement about something important
mcqs.why: In this lesson 'well' means a deep hole in the ground from which water is taken out, namely Bair-e-Roma, the well of sweet water in Madina.

mcqs.q: In the phrase 'a thousand camel-load of flour', what does 'load' mean?
options: To tell somebody about something important
The amount that is carried at one time
To reject an offer or a proposal
A lack of food over a long period
mcqs.why: Here 'load' means the amount that is carried at one time, so a thousand camel-loads means the flour that a thousand camels could carry.

mcqs.q: In this lesson, 'embraced' means that Hazrat Umar (RA) ____ Hazrat Usman (RA).
options: refused the offer of
publicly announced about
held him tightly in his arms to show love and affection
informed him about
mcqs.why: In context, 'embraced' means held someone tightly in the arms to show love and affection, as Hazrat Umar (RA) embraced Hazrat Usman (RA) after weeping.

mcqs.q: Choose the correct adverb: 'I ____ go to bed at 10 o'clock.'
options: never
usually
once
rarely
mcqs.why: The solved exercise fills this blank with 'usually', an adverb of frequency showing the habit of going to bed at 10 o'clock.

mcqs.q: Rewrite correctly: 'She is at home. (rarely)'
options: She rarely is at home
Rarely she is at home always
She is at home rarely yesterday
She is rarely at home
mcqs.why: With the verb 'is', the adverb of frequency 'rarely' is placed after it, giving the correct sentence 'She is rarely at home.'

mcqs.q: Complete with the correct form: 'Our father arrived ____ than the rest of the family. (late)'
options: later
more late
latest
lately
mcqs.why: The comparative form of 'late' is 'later', which is used here because the father's arrival is compared with the rest of the family using 'than'.

mcqs.q: Complete with the correct form: 'Your husband, Kamal, writes ____ of all. (well)'
options: better
more well
best
wellest
mcqs.why: The superlative form of 'well' is 'best', and it is required here because Kamal's writing is compared with all others, shown by the words 'of all'.

mcqs.q: The adverbial phrase in 'We expect our grandparents to arrive in about an hour' answers which question?
options: How much?
How?
When?
Where?
mcqs.why: The adverbial phrase 'in about an hour' tells the time of the expected arrival, so it answers the question 'When?'

mcqs.q: Which part is the adverb clause in 'Because no one was home, the thieves robbed the house'?
options: the thieves robbed the house
Because no one was home
robbed the house
no one was home thieves
mcqs.why: An adverb clause is a dependent clause giving a reason; 'Because no one was home' gives the reason for the robbery and is the adverb clause in this sentence.

lessons.title: Writing
lessons.notes_html:
Writing A — Essay on Generosity

  • Q: Q1. Write an essay of about 100-150 words on 'Generosity' using the mind-map given in the book.
    Ans: Generosity means being willing to give money, gifts, time and kindness freely to others. A generous person is sympathetic towards people and feels their pain as his own. He shares his money, time and energy with others to make their lives easier and pleasant. He does not give only from what is extra; he saves in order to be able to give to the needy. A generous person is also kind and encouraging in his words and behaviour. The best thing about generosity is that it expects nothing in return. Hazrat Usman (RA), who bought a well for the thirsty people of Madina and gave away his flour in the famine, is a shining example of generosity. We should also be generous so that no one around us remains in hardship.

Writing C — Helping Mankind with Inherited Money

  • Q: Q1. Your grandfather has left you money but you have to spend some amount in helping mankind / underprivileged. How will you do it?
    Ans: If my grandfather left me money and some of it had to be spent in helping mankind, I would first find out the most needy and underprivileged people around me. I would spend the amount on clean drinking water, food and medicines for poor families, and on books, uniforms and school fees for poor children. I would also help a deserving widow or a sick person who cannot pay for treatment. I would give the help quietly and respectfully, without expecting any praise or return, so that the money truly makes the lives of others easier.

Writing D — Summary of the Lesson The Two Bargains

  • Q: Q1. Write down the summary of the lesson 'The Two Bargains'.
    Ans: Arabia is a desert land where water is scarce. When the Holy Prophet (PBUH) migrated to Madina, the only well of sweet water, Bair-e-Roma, belonged to a Jew who sold its water at a high price, and the poor companions found it hard to get water. The Holy Prophet (PBUH) asked who would purchase Paradise in return for Bair-e-Roma. Hazrat Usman (RA) quietly bought half of the well for twelve thousand dirhams and allowed everyone to take water free on his day. People stored water for the next day too, so the Jew earned nothing and sold the other half as well, and the well was dedicated to the people of Madina. In the second bargain, during the famine in the days of Caliph Umar (RA), a thousand camel-loads of flour belonging to Hazrat Usman (RA) reached Madina. Hazrat Umar (RA) offered up to nine times the price, but Hazrat Usman (RA) refused, saying he had already sold the flour to Allah, who promised ten to seven hundred times the reward. The flour was then distributed among the people happily and generously.

Writing E — Read the Passage and Answer the Questions

  • Q: Q1. What is the main idea of the passage?
    Ans: The main idea of the passage is the generosity of Hazrat Usman (RA). Although the Muslims no longer had any difficulty about water, he still bought the other half of the well, paid the Jew whatever he asked, and dedicated the whole well as an endowment to the people of Madina.
  • Q: Q2. Locate at least three adjectives.
    Ans: Three adjectives in the passage are: 'bitter' (a bitter lesson), 'other' (the other half) and 'such' (such was his generosity).
  • Q: Q3. Identify the tense of the passage.
    Ans: The passage is in the past tense. Its verbs are mostly in the simple past, such as learnt, hoped, made, went, offered and paid, with some use of the past perfect, such as had hoped.
  • Q: Q4. Why did the Jew go to Hazrat Usman (RA)?
    Ans: The Jew went to Hazrat Usman (RA) to offer to sell the other half of the well also. He had earned nothing after Hazrat Usman (RA) gave water free on his day, so he wanted to sell his remaining share instead of keeping a useless bargain.

mcqs.q: According to the model essay, generosity means ____.
options: giving only when others praise us in return
being willing to give money, gifts, time and kindness freely to others
saving all our money only for ourselves
giving only what we dislike to other people
mcqs.why: The essay defines generosity as being willing to give money, gifts, time and kindness freely to others, and a generous person feels others' pain as his own.

mcqs.q: What does the model essay say is the best thing about generosity?
options: It expects nothing in return
It brings fame to the giver
It makes the giver richer in money
It is done only from extra wealth
mcqs.why: The essay says the best thing about generosity is that it expects nothing in return; a generous person helps only to make others' lives easier and pleasant.

mcqs.q: How, according to the essay, does a generous person manage to give?
options: He gives only from what is extra and never saves
He saves in order to be able to give to the needy
He borrows money from others in order to give
He gives only once in his whole life
mcqs.why: The essay states that a generous person does not give only from what is extra; he saves in order to be able to give to the needy when the need arises.

mcqs.q: Which example of generosity is given at the end of the model essay?
options: Hazrat Umar (RA) offering nine times the price of flour
The Jew selling the other half of the well
Hazrat Usman (RA), who bought a well for the thirsty people of Madina and gave away his flour in the famine
A student sharing books with his classmates
mcqs.why: The essay ends by naming Hazrat Usman (RA) as a shining example of generosity because he bought a well for the thirsty people of Madina and gave away his flour in the famine.

mcqs.q: In the model answer about spending inherited money on mankind, what should be done first?
options: Spend the money quickly before anyone asks about it
Find out the most needy and underprivileged people around us
Buy books and uniforms for our own family first
Give the money to a famous organisation only
mcqs.why: The model answer begins by finding out the most needy and underprivileged people around us, so that the inherited money reaches those who truly need help.

mcqs.q: On what would the writer of the model answer spend the inherited money?
options: Only on building a new house for himself
Only on food for poor families and nothing else
Clean drinking water, food and medicines for poor families, and books, uniforms and school fees for poor children
Only on medicines for one sick person
mcqs.why: The model answer lists clean drinking water, food and medicines for poor families, and books, uniforms and school fees for poor children, as the uses of the money.

mcqs.q: How should the help with inherited money be given, according to the model answer?
options: Publicly, so that everyone praises the giver
Quietly and respectfully, without expecting any praise or return
Only after the poor people repay part of it
Through advertisement in the newspapers
mcqs.why: The model answer says the help would be given quietly and respectfully, without expecting any praise or return, so that the money truly makes others' lives easier.

mcqs.q: According to the model summary, what happened after people stored water for the next day as well?
options: The Jew earned double profit on his own day
The well was closed for all the people of Madina
Hazrat Usman (RA) bought the well for nine thousand dirhams
The Jew earned nothing and sold the other half as well, and the well was dedicated to the people of Madina
mcqs.why: The summary explains that people stored water for the next day too, so the Jew earned nothing, sold the other half as well, and the well was dedicated to the people of Madina.

mcqs.q: According to the model summary, why did Hazrat Usman (RA) refuse Hazrat Umar's (RA) offer of up to nine times the price?
options: He wanted twenty times the price from Hazrat Umar (RA)
He had already sold the flour to Allah, who promised ten to seven hundred times the reward
He had already sold the flour to the Jew of Madina
He did not want the flour to reach the people
mcqs.why: The summary states that Hazrat Usman (RA) had already sold the flour to Allah, who promised ten to seven hundred times the reward, so no worldly offer could match it.

mcqs.q: In the passage exercise, what is the tense of the passage about the Jew and the well?
options: Present tense, with verbs like learns and hopes
Future tense, with verbs like will learn and will pay
Past tense, with verbs like learnt, hoped, made, went, offered and paid
Present perfect tense only, with no simple past verbs
mcqs.why: The passage is in the past tense; its verbs are mostly simple past such as learnt, hoped, made, went, offered and paid, with some past perfect such as 'had hoped'.
