chapters.title: Unit 8: 'Hope is the Thing with Feathers'

lessons.title: Reading and Comprehension
lessons.notes_html:
Glossary — Word Meanings

  • Q: Define 'abash'.
    Ans: To feel embarrassed and ashamed because of something that you have done.
  • Q: Define 'crumb'.
    Ans: A very small piece of food, especially of bread or cake, that has fallen off a larger piece.
  • Q: Define 'gale'.
    Ans: An extremely strong wind.
  • Q: Define 'perches'.
    Ans: Of a bird, to land and stay on a branch, etc.
  • Q: Define 'sore'.
    Ans: A part of the body that is painful, and often red, especially because of infection or because a muscle has been used too much. In the poem it means severe or painful.
  • Q: Define 'tune'.
    Ans: A series of musical notes that are sung or played in a particular order to form a piece of music.
  • Q: Define 'extremity'.
    Ans: The furthest point, end or limit of something. In the poem it means the most difficult or extreme situation.
  • Q: Define 'strangest'.
    Ans: Most unusual or surprising, especially in a way that is difficult to understand.

Comprehension A — Questions and Answers

  • Q: Q1. What is the implicit and explicit meaning of the poem 'Hope is the thing with feathers'?
    Ans: The explicit meaning is the surface picture: a little bird with feathers lives in the human soul, sings a wordless tune without ever stopping, sings sweetest in the storm, and asks for nothing in return. The implicit, deeper meaning is that hope is a living, tireless presence inside every person. It comforts us most in hard times, it cannot easily be silenced, and it gives everything freely without demanding any reward.
  • Q: Q2. What is the theme of the poem 'Hope is the Thing with Feathers'?
    Ans: The theme of the poem is the power, permanence and selflessness of hope. Dickinson shows that hope lives permanently in the soul, becomes strongest in suffering and difficulty, and never asks for anything in return. In short, hope is presented as humanity's faithful companion in every hardship.
  • Q: Q3. How does the bird react to hardships in the poem 'Hope is the Thing with Feathers'?
    Ans: The bird does not stop or fly away in hardship; instead, it sings sweetest in the gale. The poet says the storm would have to be very severe indeed to embarrass or silence this little bird, which has kept so many people warm. So, in hardships the bird of hope becomes even more active and comforting.
  • Q: Q4. Discuss how 'Hope' and 'the Thing with Feathers' are similar. What does the poem reveal about hope?
    Ans: Hope and the little bird are similar because both live close to us, both comfort us with their presence, and both keep going in bad weather and bad times. Like a bird, hope is light and gentle yet surprisingly strong and hard to destroy. The poem reveals that hope is constant, courageous and completely selfless: it never stops helping us and never asks for even a crumb in return.
  • Q: Q5. What do you understand by 'And sore must be the storm'?
    Ans: The line means that the storm would have to be extremely severe and painful to defeat hope. In other words, only the worst kind of trouble could silence the little bird that has comforted so many people. It shows how strong and unbreakable hope is.
  • Q: Q6. Do you like this poem? Why?
    Ans: Yes, I like this poem very much because it describes a deep feeling in very simple words and a beautiful image. The picture of hope as a small singing bird makes the idea easy to understand and remember. Its message, that we should never give up because hope asks for nothing and never leaves us, is encouraging for every reader.
  • Q: Q7a. Read the first stanza of the poem. Which abstract noun is described as having living characteristics?
    Ans: The abstract noun is 'hope'. It cannot be seen or touched, yet the poet describes it as a living bird with feathers.
  • Q: Q7b. What living characteristics does this item have?
    Ans: Hope is given the living characteristics of a bird: it has feathers, it perches in the soul, and it sings a tune. Singing continuously without stopping is also a living activity, so hope behaves like a living, singing creature throughout the stanza.

Comprehension B — Choose the Correct Option

  • Q: Q1. The Poet's comparison of hope to a bird is made in the form of ________.
    Options: personification / simile / alliteration / metaphor
    Ans: metaphor
  • Q: Q2. The poet uses the words 'gale' and 'storm' as metaphor. What do these words represent?
    Options: times of bad weather / hard or painful times / pleasant times / times of success and growth
    Ans: hard or painful times
  • Q: Q3. 'Hope is helpful in times of pain, sorrow and difficulty'. Which of the following lines from the poem best support this statement?
    Options: 'Hope' is the thing with feathers - That perches in the soul - / And sings the tune without the words - And never stops - at all - / And sweetest - in the Gale - is heard - And sore must be the storm - / Yet - never - in Extremity, It asked a crumb - of me.
    Ans: And sweetest - in the Gale - is heard - And sore must be the storm -
  • Q: Q4. The poet says that 'And sings the tune without the words'. Why the bird of hope sings in a tune that has no words?
    Options: to emphasize that hope does not need to be put into words to be felt / to point out that it is very difficult for people to express whether they feel hopeful or not / to suggest that people are unable to understand the feeling of hope / to indicate that people who are always hopeful are also often forgetful
    Ans: to emphasize that hope does not need to be put into words to be felt
  • Q: Q5. Read the lines: 'And sore must be the storm / That could abash the little Bird / That kept so many warm -' What does the word 'abash' mean in the above lines?
    Options: to confuse / to support / to praise / to silence
    Ans: to confuse

mcqs.q: The Poet's comparison of hope to a bird is made in the form of ________.
options: personification
simile
alliteration
metaphor
mcqs.why: Hope is directly compared to a bird with feathers without using 'like' or 'as', and a direct comparison of this kind is a metaphor, not a simile.

mcqs.q: The poet uses the words 'gale' and 'storm' as metaphor. What do these words represent?
options: times of bad weather
pleasant times
hard or painful times
times of success and growth
mcqs.why: In the poem 'gale' and 'storm' are metaphors for hard or painful times in life, against which the bird of hope sings its sweetest song.

mcqs.q: 'Hope is helpful in times of pain, sorrow and difficulty'. Which of the following lines from the poem best support this statement?
options: 'Hope' is the thing with feathers - That perches in the soul -
And sings the tune without the words - And never stops - at all -
Yet - never - in Extremity, It asked a crumb - of me.
And sweetest - in the Gale - is heard - And sore must be the storm -
mcqs.why: These lines show hope singing sweetest in the gale, that is, in hardship, and say the storm must be sore indeed to silence it, so they best support hope's help in difficulty.

mcqs.q: The poet says that 'And sings the tune without the words'. Why the bird of hope sings in a tune that has no words?
options: to point out that it is very difficult for people to express whether they feel hopeful or not
to emphasize that hope does not need to be put into words to be felt
to suggest that people are unable to understand the feeling of hope
to indicate that people who are always hopeful are also often forgetful
mcqs.why: The wordless tune emphasizes that hope does not need to be put into words to be felt; it is a living presence in the soul that comforts us silently and constantly.

mcqs.q: Read the lines: 'And sore must be the storm / That could abash the little Bird / That kept so many warm -' What does the word 'abash' mean in the above lines?
options: to support
to praise
to silence
to confuse
mcqs.why: In the book's keyed answer for these lines, 'abash' is taken as 'to confuse' the little bird; the glossary sense behind it is to embarrass or unsettle the bird that kept so many warm.

mcqs.q: What is the explicit, surface picture presented in the poem?
options: A bird flying away from the soul during a storm
A little bird with feathers that lives in the human soul, sings a wordless tune without stopping, and asks for nothing
A sailor hearing a bird sing on the strangest sea
A bird asking the poet for a crumb of bread
mcqs.why: The explicit meaning is the surface picture: a little bird with feathers lives in the human soul, sings a wordless tune without ever stopping, and asks for nothing in return.

mcqs.q: What is the theme of the poem 'Hope is the Thing with Feathers'?
options: The power, permanence and selflessness of hope
The dangers of travelling on a stormy sea
The beauty of birds in cold lands
The importance of singing without words
mcqs.why: The theme is the power, permanence and selflessness of hope: it lives permanently in the soul, becomes strongest in suffering, and never asks for anything in return.

mcqs.q: How does the bird of hope react to hardships in the poem?
options: It stops singing and flies away from the soul
It sings sweetest in the gale
It asks the poet for a crumb
It hides until the storm is over
mcqs.why: The bird does not stop or fly away in hardship; instead it sings sweetest in the gale, so in hardship hope becomes even more active and comforting.

mcqs.q: What do you understand by the line 'And sore must be the storm'?
options: The storm would have to be extremely severe and painful to defeat hope
The storm is always stronger than the little bird
The bird feels pain whenever any wind blows
Every storm can easily silence the bird of hope
mcqs.why: The line means only the worst and most severe kind of trouble could silence the little bird that has comforted so many people, which shows how strong and unbreakable hope is.

mcqs.q: Which abstract noun is described as having living characteristics in the first stanza?
options: Storm
Hope
Tune
Soul
mcqs.why: The abstract noun is 'hope': it cannot be seen or touched, yet the poet describes it as a living bird with feathers that perches in the soul and sings.

lessons.title: Language Focus
lessons.notes_html:
Vocabulary A — Connotative and Denotative Meanings

  • Q: Q1. Write the connotative and denotative meanings of 'warm'.
    Ans: Denotative meaning: having a moderately high temperature; slightly hot. Connotative meaning: comfort, safety, kindness and being cared for, as when the bird 'kept so many warm' in the poem, meaning it comforted and protected them.
  • Q: Q2. Write the connotative and denotative meanings of 'gale'.
    Ans: Denotative meaning: an extremely strong wind. Connotative meaning: trouble, hardship and painful times in life, against which hope sings the sweetest.
  • Q: Q3. Write the connotative and denotative meanings of 'sea'.
    Ans: Denotative meaning: a large area of salt water. Connotative meaning: vast, unknown and strange situations or journeys in life; the poet has heard hope even 'on the strangest Sea', meaning in the most unfamiliar circumstances.
  • Q: Q4. Write the connotative and denotative meanings of 'extremity'.
    Ans: Denotative meaning: the furthest point, end or limit of something. Connotative meaning: the worst difficulty, danger or suffering a person can face, in which hope still asks for nothing.
  • Q: Q5. Write the connotative and denotative meanings of 'chilliest'.
    Ans: Denotative meaning: the coldest, as in 'the chilliest land'. Connotative meaning: the most hopeless, lonely and unwelcoming conditions, where hope can still be heard.

Vocabulary B — Metaphor and Imagery in the Poem

  • Q: Q1. Which lines of the poem indicate metaphor and imagery?
    Ans: The whole opening is a metaphor: ''Hope' is the thing with feathers - That perches in the soul -', where hope is directly compared to a bird without using 'like' or 'as'. Imagery is created by 'And sings the tune without the words' (sound imagery), 'And sweetest - in the Gale - is heard' (sound imagery of singing in a storm), 'That kept so many warm' (touch imagery of warmth) and 'It asked a crumb - of me' (visual image of a bird asking for a tiny piece of food).

Vocabulary C — Personification, Simile, Metaphor or Imagery

  • Q: Q1. Specify whether the line represents personification, simile, metaphor or imagery: 'I wandered lonely as a cloud.'
    Ans: Simile, because the poet compares himself to a cloud using the word 'as'.
  • Q: Q2. Specify whether the line represents personification, simile, metaphor or imagery: 'He stirred his Velvet Head.'
    Ans: Imagery, because the word 'velvet' creates a picture and a feeling of softness that appeals to the senses of sight and touch.
  • Q: Q3. Specify whether the line represents personification, simile, metaphor or imagery: 'Even if they are a crowd of sorrows,'
    Ans: Metaphor, because sorrows are directly described as a crowd, as if sorrows were people gathered together.
  • Q: Q4. Specify whether the line represents personification, simile, metaphor or imagery: 'I faked a small smile and then shifted away.'
    Ans: Imagery, because the line creates a clear visual picture of a person's action and expression that we can see in our mind.
  • Q: Q5. Specify whether the line represents personification, simile, metaphor or imagery: 'Which is the bliss of solitude;'
    Ans: Metaphor, because the inward eye is directly called the bliss of solitude without using 'like' or 'as'.
  • Q: Q6. Specify whether the line represents personification, simile, metaphor or imagery: 'They looked like frightened Beads, I thought-'
    Ans: Simile, because the eyes are compared to frightened beads using the word 'like'.
  • Q: Q7. Specify whether the line represents personification, simile, metaphor or imagery: 'A host of golden daffodils;'
    Ans: Imagery, because the words create a bright visual picture of a large number of yellow daffodils that appeals to the sense of sight.
  • Q: Q8. Specify whether the line represents personification, simile, metaphor or imagery: 'This being human is a guest house.'
    Ans: Metaphor, because a human being is directly compared to a guest house without using 'like' or 'as'.
  • Q: Q9. Specify whether the line represents personification, simile, metaphor or imagery: 'The weed before me was dying or dead.'
    Ans: Imagery, because the line presents a clear visual image of a dying weed before the reader's eyes.
  • Q: Q10. Specify whether the line represents personification, simile, metaphor or imagery: 'Ten thousand saw I at a glance,'
    Ans: Imagery, because the line appeals to the sense of sight by picturing thousands of daffodils seen in a single look.

Vocabulary D — Words and Phrases from the Poem

  • Q: Q1. Which word/phrase in the poem means the same as 'react to hardships'?
    Ans: 'And sweetest - in the Gale - is heard' - hope responds to hardship by singing its sweetest song in the storm.
  • Q: Q2. Which word/phrase in the poem means the same as 'hope never stops'?
    Ans: 'And never stops - at all -'
  • Q: Q3. Which word/phrase in the poem means the same as 'found everywhere'?
    Ans: 'I've heard it in the chilliest land - And on the strangest Sea -'
  • Q: Q4. Which word/phrase in the poem means the same as 'lives in the soul'?
    Ans: 'That perches in the soul'
  • Q: Q5. Which word/phrase in the poem means the same as 'effect of hardships'?
    Ans: 'And sore must be the storm - That could abash the little Bird' - hardship is shown through the sore storm that could embarrass the bird.

Grammar A — Prepositions

  • Q: Q1. The princess lives ____ the castle.
    Ans: in
  • Q: Q2. I bought some milk ____ the grocery store.
    Ans: at
  • Q: Q3a. My sister sat ____ my mom on the bus. (first blank)
    Ans: with
  • Q: Q3b. My sister sat with my mom ____ the bus. (second blank)
    Ans: on
  • Q: Q4. When we got ready for dinner, I had to take my books ____ the table.
    Ans: from
  • Q: Q5. We took a trip ____ town last week.
    Ans: to
  • Q: Q6. He is ____ home.
    Ans: at
  • Q: Q7. Her apartment is ____ the second floor.
    Ans: on
  • Q: Q8. The boat will take you ____ the river.
    Ans: across
  • Q: Q9. The street runs ____ the seafront.
    Ans: along
  • Q: Q10. I prefer to ride my bike ____ the hill.
    Ans: down

Grammar B — Adding a Prepositional Phrase

  • Q: Q1. Rewrite the sentence adding a prepositional phrase from the list: 'The children played sea saw.'
    Ans: The children played sea saw at the park.
  • Q: Q2. Rewrite the sentence adding a prepositional phrase from the list: 'The cup cake is yours.'
    Ans: The cup cake with sprinkles is yours.
  • Q: Q3. Rewrite the sentence adding a prepositional phrase from the list: 'The lion was killed.'
    Ans: The lion was killed by the hunters.
  • Q: Q4. Rewrite the sentence adding a prepositional phrase from the list: 'We will be back.'
    Ans: We will be back in a few days.
  • Q: Q5. Rewrite the sentence adding a prepositional phrase from the list: 'Lubna rode her bicycle.'
    Ans: Lubna rode her bicycle across the yard.

Grammar C — Sentences with Prepositional Phrases

  • Q: Q1. Write a sentence using the prepositional phrase 'about the book'.
    Ans: Our teacher told us an interesting story about the book.
  • Q: Q2. Write a sentence using the prepositional phrase 'over the river'.
    Ans: The old bridge over the river connects the two villages.
  • Q: Q3. Write a sentence using the prepositional phrase 'on Tuesday'.
    Ans: We will have our English test on Tuesday.
  • Q: Q4. Write a sentence using the prepositional phrase 'by the chair'.
    Ans: He placed his school bag by the chair.

Grammar D — Prepositional Phrases and Prepositions

  • Q: Q1. Underline the prepositional phrase in the sentence and circle the preposition: 'My grandparents enjoyed boating on the beautiful lake.'
    Ans: Prepositional phrase: 'on the beautiful lake'. Preposition: 'on'.
  • Q: Q2. Underline the prepositional phrase in the sentence and circle the preposition: 'Spiders do not usually build webs in a busy area.'
    Ans: Prepositional phrase: 'in a busy area'. Preposition: 'in'.
  • Q: Q3. Underline the prepositional phrase in the sentence and circle the preposition: 'Our cricket team played well during the championship tournament.'
    Ans: Prepositional phrase: 'during the championship tournament'. Preposition: 'during'.
  • Q: Q4. Underline the prepositional phrase in the sentence and circle the preposition: 'The sun shone brightly in the afternoon.'
    Ans: Prepositional phrase: 'in the afternoon'. Preposition: 'in'.
  • Q: Q5. Underline the prepositional phrase in the sentence and circle the preposition: 'I saw a wonderful painting by Sadequain.'
    Ans: Prepositional phrase: 'by Sadequain'. Preposition: 'by'.

mcqs.q: What is the denotative meaning of 'warm'?
options: Comfort, safety and kindness
Having a moderately high temperature; slightly hot
Trouble and hardship in life
The worst difficulty a person can face
mcqs.why: The denotative meaning is the dictionary meaning: having a moderately high temperature; slightly hot. Comfort and being cared for are its connotative meanings in the poem.

mcqs.q: What is the connotative meaning of 'gale' in the poem?
options: An extremely strong wind only
A large area of salt water
Trouble, hardship and painful times in life, against which hope sings the sweetest
The furthest point or limit of something
mcqs.why: Denotatively a gale is an extremely strong wind, but connotatively in the poem it means trouble, hardship and painful times in life, against which hope sings the sweetest.

mcqs.q: What does 'sea' suggest connotatively in 'on the strangest Sea'?
options: A very small piece of bread or cake
Vast, unknown and strange situations or journeys in life
The coldest and most hopeless land
A series of musical notes sung in order
mcqs.why: Denotatively the sea is a large area of salt water, but connotatively it suggests vast, unknown and strange situations or journeys in life in which hope can still be heard.

mcqs.q: What is the connotative meaning of 'extremity' in the poem?
options: The most difficult or extreme situation; the worst difficulty, danger or suffering a person can face
A very strong wind blowing over the land
A small piece of food asked by a bird
The place where a bird lands on a branch
mcqs.why: In the poem 'extremity' connotes the worst difficulty, danger or suffering a person can face, and even in extremity hope asks for nothing in return.

mcqs.q: 'I wandered lonely as a cloud.' This line is an example of ____.
options: metaphor
imagery
simile
personification
mcqs.why: This is a simile because the poet compares himself to a cloud using the word 'as'; a comparison made with 'like' or 'as' is a simile.

mcqs.q: 'They looked like frightened Beads, I thought-' This line is an example of ____.
options: simile
metaphor
imagery
alliteration
mcqs.why: This is a simile because the eyes are compared to frightened beads using the word 'like', which is the clear sign of a simile.

mcqs.q: 'This being human is a guest house.' This line is an example of ____.
options: simile
imagery
metaphor
personification
mcqs.why: This is a metaphor because a human being is directly compared to a guest house without using 'like' or 'as', making the comparison direct.

mcqs.q: 'A host of golden daffodils;' This line is mainly an example of ____.
options: metaphor
simile
imagery
personification
mcqs.why: This is imagery because the words create a bright visual picture of a large number of yellow daffodils that appeals to the sense of sight.

mcqs.q: Which phrase in the poem means the same as 'lives in the soul'?
options: And never stops - at all -
That perches in the soul
It asked a crumb - of me
On the strangest Sea
mcqs.why: The phrase 'That perches in the soul' tells where the bird of hope lives: like a bird resting on a branch, hope perches, or lives, in the human soul.

mcqs.q: Which phrase in the poem means the same as 'hope never stops'?
options: And sweetest - in the Gale - is heard
That kept so many warm
And never stops - at all -
Yet - never - in Extremity
mcqs.why: The line 'And never stops - at all -' states directly that the bird's singing, and therefore hope itself, never stops at any time.

mcqs.q: Choose the correct preposition: 'The princess lives ____ the castle.'
options: at
in
on
across
mcqs.why: The solved exercise uses 'in' because the princess lives inside the castle, so the correct sentence is 'The princess lives in the castle.'

mcqs.q: Choose the correct preposition: 'Her apartment is ____ the second floor.'
options: in
at
on
along
mcqs.why: Floors of a building take the preposition 'on', so the solved answer is 'Her apartment is on the second floor.'

mcqs.q: Choose the correct preposition: 'The boat will take you ____ the river.'
options: down
from
across
with
mcqs.why: The boat takes you from one side of the river to the other, so the solved preposition is 'across': 'The boat will take you across the river.'

mcqs.q: Which is the prepositional phrase in 'My grandparents enjoyed boating on the beautiful lake'?
options: enjoyed boating
on the beautiful lake
My grandparents enjoyed
boating on the beautiful
mcqs.why: A prepositional phrase begins with a preposition; here the phrase is 'on the beautiful lake' and its preposition is 'on'.

mcqs.q: In 'I saw a wonderful painting by Sadequain', the preposition is ____.
options: wonderful
painting
saw
by
mcqs.why: The prepositional phrase in this sentence is 'by Sadequain', and the word that begins the phrase, 'by', is the preposition.

lessons.title: Writing
lessons.notes_html:
Writing

  • Q: Q1. Paraphrase the first and second stanza of the poem 'Hope is the Thing with Feathers.'
    Ans: Stanza 1: Hope is like a small bird with feathers that lives inside the human soul. It sings a sweet tune that has no words, and it never stops singing at any time. Stanza 2: Its song is heard at its sweetest during a strong storm, and the storm would have to be extremely severe to embarrass or silence this little bird, because this bird has given comfort and warmth to a great many people.
  • Q: Q2. Write a summary of the poem 'Hope is the Thing with Feathers.'
    Ans: In this poem Emily Dickinson compares hope to a little bird with feathers that perches in the human soul. The bird sings a wordless tune and never stops at all. Its song sounds sweetest in the gale, and only a very sore storm could abash the bird that has kept so many people warm. The poet says she has heard this bird in the chilliest land and on the strangest sea, yet even in the worst difficulty it never asked her for a single crumb. The summary of the poem is that hope is permanent, strongest in hardship, universal, and completely selfless.

mcqs.q: In the paraphrase of the first stanza, hope is described as ____.
options: a storm that troubles the human soul
a small bird with feathers that lives inside the human soul
a sailor singing on the strangest sea
a crumb of food given to a bird
mcqs.why: The paraphrase of stanza 1 says hope is like a small bird with feathers that lives inside the human soul and sings a sweet tune that has no words.

mcqs.q: According to the paraphrase, what is special about the bird's tune in the first stanza?
options: It has difficult words that nobody understands
It is sung only during a storm
It has no words, and the bird never stops singing at any time
It is heard only in the chilliest land
mcqs.why: The paraphrase explains that the bird sings a sweet tune that has no words, and it never stops singing at any time, which shows hope's constancy.

mcqs.q: In the paraphrase of the second stanza, when is the bird's song heard at its sweetest?
options: During a strong storm
In the chilliest land
On the strangest sea
When it asks for a crumb
mcqs.why: The paraphrase of stanza 2 says its song is heard at its sweetest during a strong storm, meaning hope comforts us most in hard times.

mcqs.q: According to the paraphrase of the second stanza, what kind of storm could silence the bird?
options: Any ordinary storm with strong wind
An extremely severe storm
A storm on the strangest sea only
No storm is mentioned in the stanza
mcqs.why: The paraphrase says the storm would have to be extremely severe to embarrass or silence this little bird, because the bird has given comfort and warmth to many people.

mcqs.q: According to the summary, who is the poet of 'Hope is the Thing with Feathers'?
options: William Wordsworth
Emily Dickinson
Leigh Hunt
Robert Frost
mcqs.why: The summary begins by stating that in this poem Emily Dickinson compares hope to a little bird with feathers that perches in the human soul.

mcqs.q: According to the summary, where has the poet heard the bird of hope?
options: Only in her own garden
Only on the strangest sea
In the chilliest land and on the strangest sea
Only during the sweetest storm
mcqs.why: The summary says the poet has heard this bird in the chilliest land and on the strangest sea, showing that hope is found everywhere, even in unfamiliar circumstances.

mcqs.q: According to the summary, what did the bird never do, even in the worst difficulty?
options: It never stopped singing its wordless tune
It never asked her for a single crumb
It never perched in the human soul
It never sang in the gale
mcqs.why: The summary stresses the bird's selflessness: even in the worst difficulty, in extremity, it never asked the poet for a single crumb in return.

mcqs.q: What conclusion does the summary draw about hope?
options: Hope is permanent, strongest in hardship, universal, and completely selfless
Hope is weak, temporary and found only in easy times
Hope helps only those who feed it regularly
Hope is strongest when life is pleasant and calm
mcqs.why: The summary concludes that hope is permanent, strongest in hardship, universal, and completely selfless, which sums up the whole message of Dickinson's poem.

mcqs.q: In the summary, the bird 'kept so many warm' means that hope ____.
options: raised the temperature of the cold lands
gave comfort and warmth to a great many people
asked many people for crumbs of food
sang loudly during every storm
mcqs.why: To keep so many warm means the bird of hope gave comfort and protection to a great many people, just as warmth connotes safety and being cared for.

mcqs.q: Which line is paraphrased by 'the bird has given comfort and warmth to a great many people'?
options: That perches in the soul
And sings the tune without the words
That kept so many warm
It asked a crumb - of me
mcqs.why: The paraphrase explains the line 'That kept so many warm' by saying this bird has given comfort and warmth to a great many people.

lessons.title: Practice Activities
lessons.notes_html:
Listening and Speaking

  • Q: Listening and Speaking — Share 'why we shouldn't lose hope.' Express your ideas in front of the class.
    Ans: This is an oral classroom activity with no written answer.

lessons.title: Reading and Comprehension
lessons.notes_html:
Pre-Reading

  • Q: Q1. What are the things that you should keep in mind before buying shoes?
    Ans: Before buying shoes we should keep in mind the correct size and fit, the comfort of our feet, the quality and durability of the leather and stitching, and the price. We should also check that the shoes suit the purpose for which we are buying them. Good shoes may cost more, but they last longer and do not hurt the feet.
  • Q: Q2. What kind of shoes do you like?
    Ans: I like comfortable and durable shoes, especially well-made Peshawari chappals and strong leather shoes. I prefer shoes that fit properly, look decent and can be used for a long time. Unlike fashionable but weak shoes, such shoes give real value for money.
  • Q: Q3. Where do you buy your shoes from?
    Ans: I usually buy my shoes from a trusted local shoemaker or a reliable shoe shop in the bazaar. Buying from a known shop is better because the quality can be checked and a complaint can be made if there is a fault. Model answer; students may name their own shop.

Glossary — Word Meanings

  • Q: Define 'crisp'.
    Ans: Fresh and clean; new and slightly stiff without any folds in it.
  • Q: Define 'grave'.
    Ans: A dignified seriousness due to heavy responsibilities or cares.
  • Q: Define 'contempt'.
    Ans: The feeling that somebody or something is without value and deserves no respect at all.
  • Q: Define 'bitterly'.
    Ans: In a way that shows feelings of sadness or anger.
  • Q: Define 'dictations'.
    Ans: The act of speaking or reading so that somebody can write down the words. In the story, Zarin Gul refuses to follow the dictations of the big firms.
  • Q: Define 'irrational'.
    Ans: Not based on, or not using, clear logical thought.
  • Q: Define 'starvation'.
    Ans: The state of suffering and death caused by having no food.
  • Q: Define 'tinkling'.
    Ans: Making a light high ringing sound.
  • Q: Define 'brooded'.
    Ans: To think a lot about something that makes you annoyed, anxious or upset.
  • Q: Define 'brisk'.
    Ans: Showing a desire to get things done quickly.
  • Q: Define 'nod'.
    Ans: To move your head up and down to show agreement, understanding, etc.
  • Q: Define 'wriggle'.
    Ans: To twist and turn with quick movements.
  • Q: Define 'serpentine'.
    Ans: Like a serpent or snake.
  • Q: Define 'impression'.
    Ans: An idea, a feeling or an opinion that you get about somebody or something, or that somebody or something gives you.
  • Q: Define 'craftsman'.
    Ans: A skilled person, especially one who makes beautiful things by hand.
  • Q: Define 'overused'.
    Ans: Used too much or too often.
  • Q: Define 'mysterious'.
    Ans: Difficult to understand or explain; strange.
  • Q: Define 'hesitant'.
    Ans: Slow to speak or act because you feel uncertain, embarrassed or unwilling.
  • Q: Define 'mallet'.
    Ans: A hammer with a large wooden head.
  • Q: Define 'awl'.
    Ans: A small pointed tool used for making holes, especially in leather.
  • Q: Define 'anvil'.
    Ans: An iron block on which a blacksmith puts hot pieces of metal before shaping them with a hammer.
  • Q: Define 'barren'.
    Ans: Not good enough for plants to grow on it. In the story, the rest of the shop was empty like a desert because shoes were made only to order.

Comprehension A — Questions and Answers

  • Q: Q1. Why is Zarin Gul different from other businessmen?
    Ans: Zarin Gul is different because he is an artist, not an ordinary businessman. He does not work for profit, advertisement or quick money; he makes only ordered shoes, never compromises on quality, and refuses advance payment until the shoes are ready. He even offers to return the full amount if a pair turns out to be bad, and he refuses to become a machine in a big firm.
  • Q: Q2. How did the author come in touch with the Zarin Gul Brothers?
    Ans: The author first came in touch with Zarin Gul Brothers in his youthful days, in the holy month of Ramazan. His father took him to the shop in Qissa Khawani Bazar to order a pair of new shoes for the coming Eid. From that first visit, the author remained Zarin Gul's customer and admirer.
  • Q: Q3. Describe the shoemaker and his shop.
    Ans: Zarin Gul was an old, dignified craftsman whose remarks about shoemaking were authoritative and final; when the author met him again he was sixty-five, worn and torn like an overused pair of shoes, yet his handshake was as tight as before. His shop stood in a small but busy street of Qissa Khawani Bazar, with a monstrous black Peshawari Chappal hanging on its faint coloured wooden door. Inside it was quiet and serene like a sacred place, with old wooden stools, a few pairs of shoes in the window, and on the right side a big smooth square stone, a heavy wooden mallet, an awl and a three-legged anvil; the rest was barren because he made only ordered shoes.
  • Q: Q4. What were Zarin Gul's priorities in making shoes?
    Ans: Zarin Gul's priorities were perfect fit, comfort and extraordinary durability. His shoes never failed to fit the feet and lasted much longer than usual, because, as the author says, durability was stitched into them. Quality and his self-respect as an artist came before money, advertisement and quantity.
  • Q: Q5. What is the setting of the story?
    Ans: The setting of the story is Peshawar, mainly Zarin Gul's small shoe shop in a busy street of Qissa Khawani Bazar. The story moves between the author's youth, when his father first took him there in Ramazan for Eid shoes, and his return to Peshawar after several years abroad. The quiet, almost empty shop, contrasted with the branded shop that replaces it at the end, is the centre of the whole story.
  • Q: Q6. What is the conflict about in the story?
    Ans: The conflict is between the true craftsman and the big shoe-making companies. Zarin Gul believes shoemaking is an art based on skill, experience and self-respect, while the big firms work through advertisement, use craftsmen only for their hands, and have taken away the small craftsman's work. This conflict destroys Zarin Gul's trade and finally leads to his death by slow starvation.
  • Q: Q7. What was the author's opinion about Zarin Gul as a shoe maker?
    Ans: The author has the highest opinion of Zarin Gul as a shoemaker. He calls him 'the fantastic shoemaker' and says that to make such shoes seemed mysterious and wonderful to him then and still seems so. He believes Zarin Gul's shoes never failed to fit and lasted extraordinarily long, and he fully respects his honesty and artistry.
  • Q: Q8. Why did the author visit the shop after a long time?
    Ans: The author had gone abroad for higher studies and his career and could not meet Zarin Gul for several years. When he returned to Peshawar, the first shop he went to was his old friend Zarin Gul's. He visited out of old attachment and respect, and also because he wanted shoes made by him again.
  • Q: Q9. What was Zarin Gul's complaint against 'big firms'?
    Ans: Zarin Gul complained that the big firms had extended their tentacles into the shoemaking trade and had hired the craftsmen. He said, 'These big firms use their hands not their brain or experience,' and that the companies get everything 'by advertisement, not by work.' His bitter complaint was: 'They took it away from us and presently we have no work.'
  • Q: Q10. Retell the story in the form of a dialogue.
    Ans: Author: Zarin Gul Kaka, isn't it awfully hard to make shoes in such tough conditions? Zarin Gul: It is an art. Author (years later): Kaka, do you want to make shoes for me? I can pay in advance. Zarin Gul: Those are not my shoes. Do the big shoe-making companies have no self-respect? I am an artist, not a machine who will blindly follow their irrational and stupid dictations. They get it all by advertisement, not by work. Pay when the shoes are ready to deliver. Young man at the shop (a week later): No sir, Zarin Gul is dead. Poor old man starved himself. Slow starvation, the doctor called it. This dialogue retells the meeting, the complaint against the big firms, the refusal of advance payment, and the sad end of the fantastic shoemaker.

Comprehension B — Choose the Best Option

  • Q: Q1. Zarin Gul Brothers' shoes were extremely durable because he never compromised on _________________.
    Options: money / quality / labour / quantity
    Ans: quality
  • Q: Q2. 'It is an art!' About what did Zarin Gul say so?
    Options: dealing with clients / shoe / chappal making / competition with big firms / advertisement of shops and products
    Ans: shoe / chappal making
  • Q: Q3. 'I was again in Peshawar....' In this sentence 'I' refers to __________.
    Options: Zarin Gul's elder brother / the author / the author's father / Zarin Gul
    Ans: the author
  • Q: Q4. Zarin Gul Brothers was taken by a new firm because ____________.
    Options: Zarin Gul died of starvation / Zarin Gul never advertised his shop and products / the new firm produced better quality shoes / Zarin Gul produced poor quality shoes
    Ans: Zarin Gul died of starvation

mcqs.q: Zarin Gul Brothers' shoes were extremely durable because he never compromised on _________________.
options: money
labour
quality
quantity
mcqs.why: Zarin Gul's shoes lasted extraordinarily long because durability was stitched into them; he never compromised on quality, which always came before money and quantity.

mcqs.q: 'It is an art!' About what did Zarin Gul say so?
options: dealing with clients
competition with big firms
advertisement of shops and products
shoe / chappal making
mcqs.why: When the author asked whether it was not awfully hard to make shoes in such tough conditions, Zarin Gul replied 'It is an art!', speaking about shoe and chappal making.

mcqs.q: 'I was again in Peshawar....' In this sentence 'I' refers to __________.
options: Zarin Gul's elder brother
the author's father
the author
Zarin Gul
mcqs.why: The story is narrated in the first person by the author, so 'I was again in Peshawar' refers to the author returning after several years abroad.

mcqs.q: Zarin Gul Brothers was taken by a new firm because ____________.
options: Zarin Gul never advertised his shop and products
Zarin Gul died of starvation
the new firm produced better quality shoes
Zarin Gul produced poor quality shoes
mcqs.why: When the author returned a week later, the shop had been taken over by a new firm because Zarin Gul had died of slow starvation, having spent everything on rent and leather.

mcqs.q: Why is Zarin Gul different from other businessmen?
options: He worked only for profit and quick money
He advertised his shoes in every bazaar
He treated shoemaking as an art, made only ordered shoes and refused advance payment until the shoes were ready
He employed many craftsmen in a big firm
mcqs.why: Zarin Gul is different because he is an artist, not an ordinary businessman: he makes only ordered shoes, never compromises on quality, and refuses advance payment until the shoes are ready.

mcqs.q: How did the author first come in touch with the Zarin Gul Brothers?
options: His father took him to the shop in Qissa Khawani Bazar in Ramazan to order new shoes for Eid
He met Zarin Gul abroad during his higher studies
A big firm introduced him to the shoemaker
He ordered shoes from the shop by advertisement
mcqs.why: The author first came in touch with Zarin Gul Brothers in his youthful days, in the holy month of Ramazan, when his father took him to the shop to order new shoes for the coming Eid.

mcqs.q: How is Zarin Gul described when the author met him again after many years?
options: Young, rich and brisk like a new businessman
Sixty-five, worn and torn like an overused pair of shoes, yet with a handshake as tight as before
A manager of a big multinational shoe firm
Hesitant and unable to recognise the author
mcqs.why: When the author met him again, Zarin Gul was sixty-five, worn and torn like an overused pair of shoes, yet his handshake was as tight as before.

mcqs.q: What were Zarin Gul's priorities in making shoes?
options: Advertisement, quantity and quick profit
Low price, fashion and large stock
Perfect fit, comfort and extraordinary durability
Following the dictations of the big firms
mcqs.why: Zarin Gul's priorities were perfect fit, comfort and extraordinary durability; his shoes never failed to fit and lasted much longer than usual because quality came before money.

mcqs.q: What is the setting of the story 'The Fantastic Shoemaker'?
options: A big shoe factory in a foreign country
Peshawar, mainly Zarin Gul's small shoe shop in a busy street of Qissa Khawani Bazar
A branded shop that replaced the old shop at the start
The author's school in his youthful days
mcqs.why: The setting is Peshawar, mainly Zarin Gul's small shoe shop in a small but busy street of Qissa Khawani Bazar, with its black Peshawari Chappal hanging on the door.

mcqs.q: What was Zarin Gul's complaint against the big firms?
options: They paid craftsmen too much money for their work
They produced shoes of better quality than his
They used craftsmen's hands, not their brain or experience, and got everything by advertisement, not by work
They refused to sell leather to small shoemakers
mcqs.why: Zarin Gul complained that the big firms had hired the craftsmen but used only their hands, not their brain or experience, and that the companies get everything by advertisement, not by work.

lessons.title: Language Focus
lessons.notes_html:
Vocabulary A — Direct Quotations

  • Q: Q1. Find and underline the direct quotations enclosed in quotation marks from the context.
    Ans: Direct quotations from the story include: 'Isn't it awfully hard to make shoes in such tough conditions?' 'It is an art.' 'Zarin Gul Kaka, my last pair of shoes makes a creaking sound, you know.' 'It shouldn't have creaked.' 'Send them back, I will look at them.' 'Some shoes are bad from birth. If I can do nothing with them, I will give back the amount you paid for them.' 'Do you want any shoes?' 'Those are not my shoes.' 'Do the big shoe-making companies have no self-respect?' 'I am an artist not machine who will blindly follow their irrational and stupid dictations.'

Vocabulary B — Sentences with Adverbs

  • Q: Q1. Rewrite a sentence from the story which has an adverb (1 of 5).
    Ans: 'It was not possible to go to him often because there was something in his shoes that was beyond the temporary.' Adverb: often.
  • Q: Q2. Rewrite a sentence from the story which has an adverb (2 of 5).
    Ans: 'The shoes that Zarin Gul made never failed to fit in the feet and they lasted extraordinarily longer than usual.' Adverbs: never, extraordinarily.
  • Q: Q3. Rewrite a sentence from the story which has an adverb (3 of 5).
    Ans: 'And then he spoke bitterly against the big multi-nationals that have extended their tentacles to the shoe-making trade.' Adverb: bitterly.
  • Q: Q4. Rewrite a sentence from the story which has an adverb (4 of 5).
    Ans: 'I can make them quickly, because I have plenty of free time.' Adverb: quickly.
  • Q: Q5. Rewrite a sentence from the story which has an adverb (5 of 5).
    Ans: 'He never gave himself time to eat; never had a penny in the house.' Adverb: never. Other adverbs in the story include again, abroad and presently.

Vocabulary C — Phrasal Verbs with 'Look'

  • Q: Q1. Give the meaning of the phrase 'look up'.
    Ans: To search for information in a book or on a computer; to consult a reference.
  • Q: Q2. Use 'look up' in a sentence of your own.
    Ans: When you feel lost, look up the word in a good dictionary.
  • Q: Q3. Give the meaning of the phrase 'look down'.
    Ans: To think that somebody is less important than you; to treat someone with contempt. It can also mean to look towards the ground.
  • Q: Q4. Use 'look down' in a sentence of your own.
    Ans: We should never look down on poor craftsmen like Zarin Gul, who work with honesty and skill.
  • Q: Q5. Give the meaning of the phrase 'look after'.
    Ans: To take care of somebody or something.
  • Q: Q6. Use 'look after' in a sentence of your own.
    Ans: My elder sister looks after our grandfather when he is ill.
  • Q: Q7. Give the meaning of the phrase 'look in'.
    Ans: To visit a place or person for a short time.
  • Q: Q8. Use 'look in' in a sentence of your own.
    Ans: On my way home, I looked in at Zarin Gul's shop to meet him.
  • Q: Q9. Give the meaning of the phrase 'look out'.
    Ans: To watch what is happening and be careful; also used as a warning to be careful.
  • Q: Q10. Use 'look out' in a sentence of your own.
    Ans: Look out! A speedy rickshaw is coming round the corner.

Grammar — Simple, Compound and Complex Sentences

  • Q: Q1. Identify the sentence as simple, compound or complex: 'This is a simple sentence.'
    Ans: Simple. It has only one independent clause with a single subject and predicate.
  • Q: Q2. Identify the sentence as simple, compound or complex: 'I like playing basketball, and my brother likes playing tennis.'
    Ans: Compound. It joins two independent clauses with the coordinating conjunction 'and'.
  • Q: Q3. Identify the sentence as simple, compound or complex: 'I'll help you if you help me.'
    Ans: Complex. It has the independent clause 'I'll help you' and the dependent clause 'if you help me'.
  • Q: Q4. Identify the sentence as simple, compound or complex: 'Her name is Sachiko and she comes from Japan.'
    Ans: Compound. It joins two independent clauses, 'Her name is Sachiko' and 'she comes from Japan', with 'and'.
  • Q: Q5. Identify the sentence as simple, compound or complex: 'My mother cooked dinner while I was doing my homework.'
    Ans: Complex. It has the independent clause 'My mother cooked dinner' and the dependent clause 'while I was doing my homework'.
  • Q: Q6. Identify the sentence as simple, compound or complex: 'While the dog chased the cat, it barked loudly.'
    Ans: Complex. It has the dependent clause 'While the dog chased the cat' and the independent clause 'it barked loudly'.
  • Q: Q7. Identify the sentence as simple, compound or complex: 'Although he worked hard, he did not do well in the examination.'
    Ans: Complex. It has the dependent clause 'Although he worked hard' and the independent clause 'he did not do well in the examination'.
  • Q: Q8. Identify the sentence as simple, compound or complex: 'The boy did not go to the zoo because they went to the park.'
    Ans: Complex. As printed, it contains the dependent clause 'because they went to the park' attached to the independent clause 'The boy did not go to the zoo', so it is a complex sentence.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a direct quotation from the story?
options: It is an art.
He spoke bitterly against the big firms.
The shoes lasted extraordinarily longer than usual.
Zarin Gul refused advance payment.
mcqs.why: 'It is an art.' is Zarin Gul's own spoken words, enclosed in quotation marks in the story, so it is a direct quotation, unlike the narrator's reported statements.

mcqs.q: What did Zarin Gul promise if a pair of his shoes turned out to be bad?
options: He would advertise the pair in the bazaar
He would give back the amount paid for them
He would make the customer wait for a year
He would send the pair to a big firm
mcqs.why: Zarin Gul said, 'Some shoes are bad from birth. If I can do nothing with them, I will give back the amount you paid for them,' showing his honesty as a craftsman.

mcqs.q: What is the adverb in 'It was not possible to go to him often because there was something in his shoes that was beyond the temporary'?
options: possible
often
temporary
something
mcqs.why: The adverb in this sentence from the story is 'often', which tells how frequently it was possible to go to Zarin Gul.

mcqs.q: Which adverbs appear in 'The shoes that Zarin Gul made never failed to fit in the feet and they lasted extraordinarily longer than usual'?
options: never and extraordinarily
fit and lasted
shoes and feet
longer and usual
mcqs.why: The adverbs in this sentence are 'never', telling when the shoes failed, and 'extraordinarily', telling how much longer the shoes lasted than usual.

mcqs.q: 'Look up' means ____.
options: to treat someone with contempt
to take care of somebody or something
to search for information in a book or on a computer; to consult a reference
to visit a place or person for a short time
mcqs.why: The phrasal verb 'look up' means to search for information in a book or on a computer, as in looking up a word in a good dictionary.

mcqs.q: 'Look down' on somebody means ____.
options: to watch what is happening and be careful
to think that somebody is less important than you; to treat someone with contempt
to take care of somebody when he is ill
to search for information in a reference book
mcqs.why: 'Look down' means to think somebody is less important than you and to treat him with contempt, which is why we should never look down on poor craftsmen like Zarin Gul.

mcqs.q: 'Look after' means ____.
options: to visit a place for a short time
to be careful and watch what is happening
to take care of somebody or something
to look towards the ground only
mcqs.why: The phrasal verb 'look after' means to take care of somebody or something, as in a sister looking after her grandfather when he is ill.

mcqs.q: 'Look in' means ____.
options: to visit a place or person for a short time
to treat someone with contempt
to consult a dictionary or reference
to take care of somebody or something
mcqs.why: 'Look in' means to visit a place or person for a short time, as in looking in at Zarin Gul's shop on the way home to meet him.

mcqs.q: 'Look out' is used to mean ____.
options: search for information in a book
watch what is happening and be careful; it is also a warning to be careful
take care of an ill person
visit somebody for a short time
mcqs.why: 'Look out' means to watch what is happening and be careful, and it is also used as a warning, as in 'Look out! A speedy rickshaw is coming round the corner.'

mcqs.q: 'This is a simple sentence.' This sentence is ____.
options: compound, because it has two independent clauses
complex, because it has a dependent clause
simple, because it has only one independent clause with a single subject and predicate
compound, because it is joined by 'and'
mcqs.why: It is a simple sentence because it has only one independent clause with a single subject and predicate, and no other clause is joined to it.

mcqs.q: Which sentence is a compound sentence?
options: I'll help you if you help me.
I like playing basketball, and my brother likes playing tennis.
My mother cooked dinner while I was doing my homework.
While the dog chased the cat, it barked loudly.
mcqs.why: This is a compound sentence because it joins two independent clauses, 'I like playing basketball' and 'my brother likes playing tennis', with the coordinating conjunction 'and'.

mcqs.q: Which sentence is a complex sentence?
options: Her name is Sachiko and she comes from Japan.
This is a simple sentence.
I like playing basketball, and my brother likes playing tennis.
I'll help you if you help me.
mcqs.why: This is a complex sentence because it has the independent clause 'I'll help you' and the dependent clause 'if you help me' joined to it.

mcqs.q: 'My mother cooked dinner while I was doing my homework.' This sentence is ____.
options: simple, because it has one clause only
complex, because it has an independent clause and the dependent clause 'while I was doing my homework'
compound, because two clauses are joined by 'and'
simple, because 'while' is a coordinating conjunction
mcqs.why: It is complex: 'My mother cooked dinner' is the independent clause and 'while I was doing my homework' is the dependent clause attached to it.

mcqs.q: 'Her name is Sachiko and she comes from Japan.' This sentence is ____.
options: complex, because of the clause 'she comes from Japan'
simple, because it has a single subject
compound, because it joins two independent clauses with 'and'
complex, because it begins with a dependent clause
mcqs.why: It is a compound sentence because it joins two independent clauses, 'Her name is Sachiko' and 'she comes from Japan', with the coordinating conjunction 'and'.

mcqs.q: What is the adverb in 'And then he spoke bitterly against the big multi-nationals'?
options: spoke
against
bitterly
then he spoke
mcqs.why: The adverb in this sentence from the story is 'bitterly', which tells how Zarin Gul spoke against the big multinational firms, in a way showing sadness and anger.

lessons.title: Writing
lessons.notes_html:
Writing

  • Q: Q1. Write down the summary of the story 'The Fantastic Shoemaker'.
    Ans: The narrator first met Zarin Gul, the fantastic shoemaker of Qissa Khawani Bazar, Peshawar, as a young boy when his father took him for Eid shoes. Zarin Gul's shoes always fitted perfectly and lasted extraordinarily long, because he treated shoemaking as an art and never compromised on quality; he even offered to refund the money for a pair that creaked. After studying abroad for years, the narrator returned to find Zarin Gul aged sixty-five, with almost no work, because big multinational firms had taken over the trade through advertisement and had reduced craftsmen to mere hands. Proud Zarin Gul refused to join them, saying he was an artist, not a machine, and he also refused the narrator's advance payment. A week later the narrator found the shop taken over by a famous brand and learned that Zarin Gul had died of slow starvation, having spent everything on rent and leather. The story is a tribute to the honest craftsman destroyed by big business.
  • Q: Q2. Write a story of at least 100 words with the help of the following beginning: 'It was a stormy night. Saad was sleeping in his bedroom. All of a sudden ...' Use appropriate similes and metaphors for comparison and contrast and connectives of comparison and contrast.
    Ans: It was a stormy night. Saad was sleeping in his bedroom. All of a sudden, a loud crash, like a clap of thunder falling in the courtyard, woke him up. The wind was howling like a hungry wolf, but unlike other nights, the house felt strangely silent inside. Saad's heart was a drum beating fast. He picked up his torch and went towards the kitchen, where a faint light was trembling. However, when he opened the door, he found only his little sister, who had come to drink water and had dropped a steel glass. Whereas Saad had imagined a thief, it was only his own fear that had frightened him. He laughed, gave her water, and went back to bed, while the storm outside slowly calmed down. That night he learnt that courage is not the absence of fear, but facing it bravely.
  • Q: Q3. Write a personal narrative / autobiography.
    Ans: I was born in a small town and brought up in a loving family. My father is a schoolteacher and my mother looks after our home. My first day at school is still fresh in my memory: I was shy and hesitant, but my kind teacher made me feel at home, and I soon began to love reading. As I grew up, I learnt honesty and hard work from my parents, just as Zarin Gul learnt his art with patience and self-respect. Winning the first prize in an essay competition in Class 8 was the happiest moment of my school life, because it proved that sincere effort is never wasted. Today I am a student of Class 9, and my aim is to become a good teacher who serves others with honesty. This is the simple story of my life so far, written by myself in the first person, in the order in which the events happened.

mcqs.q: According to the model summary, how did the narrator first meet Zarin Gul?
options: As a young boy, when his father took him to the shop in Qissa Khawani Bazar for Eid shoes
As a student abroad, in a foreign shoe shop
As a manager of a famous shoe brand
As a craftsman working in the same bazaar
mcqs.why: The summary begins by saying the narrator first met Zarin Gul as a young boy when his father took him for Eid shoes to the shop in Qissa Khawani Bazar, Peshawar.

mcqs.q: According to the summary, what did Zarin Gul offer if a pair of his shoes creaked?
options: He offered to advertise the pair free of cost
He offered to refund the money for the pair
He offered to join a big firm for repairs
He offered a second pair at half price
mcqs.why: The summary says Zarin Gul treated shoemaking as an art and never compromised on quality; he even offered to refund the money for a pair that creaked.

mcqs.q: According to the summary, what did the narrator find when he returned after studying abroad for years?
options: Zarin Gul had become the owner of a big firm
Zarin Gul had left Peshawar for another city
Zarin Gul, aged sixty-five, had almost no work because big multinational firms had taken over the trade through advertisement
Zarin Gul's shop had become the busiest shop in the bazaar
mcqs.why: The summary says the narrator returned to find Zarin Gul aged sixty-five with almost no work, because big multinational firms had taken over the trade through advertisement.

mcqs.q: According to the summary, how did Zarin Gul respond to the narrator's offer of advance payment?
options: He accepted it gladly and asked for more
He refused it; payment was to be made when the shoes were ready
He asked the narrator to pay a big firm instead
He doubled the price of the shoes at once
mcqs.why: Proud Zarin Gul refused the narrator's advance payment, saying he was an artist, not a machine; in his practice, payment came only when the shoes were ready to deliver.

mcqs.q: According to the summary, how does the story end?
options: Zarin Gul became famous through advertisement
The narrator opened a new shop for Zarin Gul
Zarin Gul had died of slow starvation, having spent everything on rent and leather, and a famous brand had taken over the shop
Zarin Gul agreed to work for a multinational firm
mcqs.why: The summary ends with the narrator finding the shop taken over by a famous brand and learning that Zarin Gul had died of slow starvation, having spent everything on rent and leather.

mcqs.q: In the model story about Saad, 'a loud crash, like a clap of thunder falling in the courtyard' is an example of ____.
options: a metaphor, because the crash is directly called thunder
a simile, because the crash is compared to thunder using 'like'
imagery only, with no comparison at all
a connective of contrast
mcqs.why: This is a simile because the loud crash is compared to a clap of thunder using the word 'like', one of the comparison devices the story was required to use.

mcqs.q: In the model story, 'The wind was howling like a hungry wolf' is ____.
options: a metaphor without any comparison word
a connective of comparison
a simile comparing the wind to a hungry wolf using 'like'
a summary of the whole story
mcqs.why: The wind is compared to a hungry wolf with the help of the word 'like', so this is a simile used for comparison in the stormy-night story.

mcqs.q: In the model story, 'Saad's heart was a drum beating fast' is an example of ____.
options: a simile, because it uses the word 'like'
a metaphor, because the heart is directly described as a drum without 'like' or 'as'
a connective of contrast such as 'whereas'
a phrasal verb with 'look'
mcqs.why: This is a metaphor because Saad's heart is directly described as a drum without using 'like' or 'as', showing how fast it beat with fear.

mcqs.q: Which word in the model story is a connective of contrast in 'Whereas Saad had imagined a thief, it was only his own fear'?
options: imagined
Whereas
fear
only
mcqs.why: 'Whereas' is a connective of contrast: it contrasts what Saad had imagined, a thief, with the reality that only his own fear had frightened him.

mcqs.q: What does the model personal narrative say about its own form?
options: It is written in the third person about another person
It is a dialogue between the author and Zarin Gul
It is written by the writer himself in the first person, in the order in which the events happened
It is a summary of somebody else's life story
mcqs.why: The model autobiography closes by stating it is the simple story of the writer's own life so far, written by himself in the first person, in the order in which the events happened.

lessons.notes_html:
Listening and Speaking
